lessons.title: Meet your first SELECT
lessons.reason: Two projections reinforce column selection before filters; small customer and product schemas remain appropriate.
lessons.concept: A table is a collection of rows and named columns. SELECT chooses the columns you want to see; FROM names the table. A query reads data without changing it.
lessons.example:
SELECT name, city
FROM store_customers;

walkthrough.title: Start with a table
walkthrough.description: Every row is one customer. Read all columns first.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM store_customers;

walkthrough.title: Choose two columns
walkthrough.description: SELECT changes the visible columns, not the underlying rows.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name,city FROM store_customers;

hints: Name the two columns after SELECT, separated by a comma.
Use FROM store_customers for the first challenge; FROM store_products for the second.

quiz.q: SELECT name FROM store_customers returns what?
options: Every customer row, with only the name column
quiz.why: SELECT chooses columns. DISTINCT, WHERE, and aggregates change other aspects of the result.

challenges.prompt: Show the name and city of every customer.
challenges.answer: SELECT name, city FROM store_customers

challenges.prompt: Show the name and price of every product.
challenges.answer: SELECT name, price FROM store_products

lessons.title: Aliases & calculated columns
lessons.reason: Transfers a calculated alias from money to quantity without introducing aggregation; quiz distinguishes output from mutation.
lessons.concept: AS gives an output column a readable name. You can calculate values for each row with arithmetic. The original table stays unchanged.
lessons.example:
SELECT name, price * 2 AS double_price
FROM store_products;

walkthrough.title: Name a calculated column
walkthrough.description: Read the stored price first. The next step multiplies it and names the result without changing the table.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, price FROM store_products;

walkthrough.title: Run the reference
walkthrough.description: AS gives an output column a readable name. You can calculate values for each row with arithmetic. The original table stays unchanged.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT name, price * 2 AS double_price
FROM store_products;

hints: Use multiplication in SELECT.
Use AS to name the calculated column exactly as requested.

quiz.q: What does price * 2 AS double_price do?
options: Updates the stored price in store_products
Returns a calculated column named double_price without changing store_products
quiz.why: AS names the output column. Arithmetic in SELECT does not update the stored price.

challenges.prompt: Return name and price * 2 as double_price for every product.
challenges.answer: SELECT name, price*2 AS double_price FROM store_products

challenges.prompt: Return id and quantity * 10 as units_times_ten for every order.
challenges.answer: SELECT id, quantity*10 AS units_times_ten FROM store_orders

lessons.title: Filter with WHERE
lessons.reason: Replaces a second city-equality task with status filtering on purchase lines; changes the row grain without a syntax jump.
lessons.concept: WHERE keeps only rows for which a condition is true. The condition can use a column that is not selected. Read the table grain before deciding which rows to keep.
lessons.example: SELECT id,status FROM store_orders WHERE status='paid'

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One customer in the first task; one purchase line in the second.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM store_orders LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,status FROM store_orders WHERE status='paid'

hints: Place WHERE after FROM.
Filter the status column while returning the purchase-line identifier.

quiz.q: What does WHERE city = 'Chicago' keep?
options: Every customer, with the city column renamed
quiz.why: WHERE keeps rows whose condition is true. The quoted text is a city value, not a new column name.

challenges.prompt: Show name and city for store_customers in Chicago.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,city FROM store_customers WHERE city='Chicago'

challenges.prompt: Show id and quantity for cancelled purchase lines in store_orders.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,quantity FROM store_orders WHERE status='cancelled'

lessons.title: Comparisons & ranges
lessons.reason: Single lower bound transfers to an inclusive two-sided range; exact endpoints matter.
lessons.concept: Use >, >=, < and <= to compare values. BETWEEN includes both endpoints. Decide whether the task includes the boundary before choosing an operator.
lessons.example:
SELECT name, price FROM store_products
WHERE price >= 45;

walkthrough.title: Include the boundary
walkthrough.description: Look at the prices. A product at exactly 45 stays when the condition uses >=.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, price FROM store_products ORDER BY price;

walkthrough.title: Run the reference
walkthrough.description: Use >, >=, < and <= to compare values. BETWEEN includes both endpoints. Decide whether the task includes the boundary before choosing an operator.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT name, price FROM store_products
WHERE price >= 45;

hints: At least means >=. BETWEEN is inclusive.
Compare the price column to numeric values.

quiz.q: Which condition keeps store_products priced 45 and above?
quiz.why: >= includes the boundary. > drops a product whose price is exactly 45.

challenges.prompt: Show name and price for store_products priced at least 45.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,price FROM store_products WHERE price>=45

challenges.prompt: Show name and price for store_products priced between 12 and 80 inclusive.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,price FROM store_products WHERE price BETWEEN 12 AND 80

lessons.title: Combine conditions
lessons.reason: Conjunction transfers to a grouped disjunction; parentheses and precedence add useful reasoning.
lessons.concept: AND requires both conditions. OR requires either. AND binds more tightly than OR, so parentheses make mixed conditions explicit.
lessons.example:
SELECT name, price FROM store_products
WHERE category = 'Tech' AND price < 100;

walkthrough.title: Require both conditions
walkthrough.description: Category and price are separate columns. AND keeps a row only when both are true.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, category, price FROM store_products;

walkthrough.title: Run the reference
walkthrough.description: AND requires both conditions. OR requires either. AND binds more tightly than OR, so parentheses make mixed conditions explicit.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT name, price FROM store_products
WHERE category = 'Tech' AND price < 100;

hints: Use AND when both conditions must be true.
Group the two categories with parentheses before applying the price condition.

quiz.q: Which rows does category = 'Tech' AND price < 100 keep?
options: Every Tech product, plus anything priced under 100
Products that are both Tech and priced under 100
Products that are Tech or priced under 100
quiz.why: AND requires both conditions on the same row. OR would keep a row that meets either one.

challenges.prompt: Show name and price for Tech store_products costing less than 100.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,price FROM store_products WHERE category='Tech' AND price<100

challenges.prompt: Show name and price for Home or Stationery store_products costing at least 12.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,price FROM store_products WHERE (category='Home' OR category='Stationery') AND price>=12

lessons.title: Lists & text patterns
lessons.reason: Prefix matching transfers to an explicit membership list; neither requires joins.
lessons.concept: IN matches any member of a list. LIKE matches text patterns: % means any number of characters and _ means one character. SQLite LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII by default.
lessons.example:
SELECT name FROM store_customers
WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

walkthrough.title: Match the start of a name
walkthrough.description: In LIKE, % stands for the rest of the name. It is not a character stored in the table.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name FROM store_customers;

walkthrough.title: Run the reference
walkthrough.description: IN matches any member of a list. LIKE matches text patterns: % means any number of characters and _ means one character. SQLite LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII by default.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT name FROM store_customers
WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

hints: A prefix pattern ends with %.
Use IN with a parenthesized list of quoted cities.

quiz.q: What does name LIKE 'A%' match?
options: Names that contain a percent sign
quiz.why: In LIKE, % stands for any number of characters. An equality comparison would look for a literal percent sign.

challenges.prompt: Show name for store_customers whose name starts with A.
challenges.answer: SELECT name FROM store_customers WHERE name LIKE 'A%'

challenges.prompt: Show name and city for store_customers in Austin or Seattle.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,city FROM store_customers WHERE city IN ('Austin','Seattle')

lessons.title: Understand NULL
lessons.reason: Detection of missing values transfers to display fallback; quiz checks UNKNOWN rather than treating NULL as text.
lessons.concept: NULL means missing or unknown. NULL = NULL is unknown, not true. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument.
lessons.example:
SELECT name, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS city
FROM store_customers;

walkthrough.title: Find missing cities
walkthrough.description: Some city values are blank in the sense of NULL. Equality to NULL never matches; IS NULL does.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, city FROM store_customers WHERE city IS NULL;

walkthrough.title: Replace NULL for display
walkthrough.description: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument. Missing cities become the label Unknown without changing stored rows.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS city FROM store_customers;

hints: Do not use = NULL.
Use IS NULL to find missing values, or COALESCE to replace them.

quiz.q: What happens when WHERE city = NULL is evaluated?
options: The comparison is unknown; those rows are not kept
quiz.why: Use IS NULL for missing values. Ordinary comparisons with NULL evaluate to unknown.

challenges.prompt: Show name for store_customers whose city is missing.
challenges.answer: SELECT name FROM store_customers WHERE city IS NULL

challenges.prompt: Return name and city, replacing missing city with Unknown (alias the column city).
challenges.answer: SELECT name,COALESCE(city,'Unknown') AS city FROM store_customers

lessons.title: Sort & limit
lessons.reason: Descending and ascending limits are intentional early repetition; the quiz introduces deterministic tie-breaking.
lessons.concept: ORDER BY sorts the output; ASC is ascending and DESC descending. LIMIT keeps a number of rows after sorting. Use a secondary key when ties need deterministic ordering.
lessons.example:
SELECT name, price FROM store_products
ORDER BY price DESC, name ASC LIMIT 3;

walkthrough.title: Sort prices before cutting
walkthrough.description: ORDER BY decides which rows come first. LIMIT only makes sense after the sort, or you get an arbitrary cut.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, price FROM store_products ORDER BY price DESC, name ASC;

walkthrough.title: Keep the top of the sorted list
walkthrough.description: DESC puts expensive store_products first. LIMIT 3 keeps only the first three after sorting.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, price FROM store_products ORDER BY price DESC, name ASC LIMIT 3;

hints: Sort by price, then use LIMIT.
Most expensive needs DESC; cheapest needs ASC.

quiz.q: How do you return the three cheapest store_products consistently?
quiz.why: Ascending price puts cheaper store_products first. id breaks equal-price ties; LIMIT keeps three rows.

challenges.prompt: Show name and price of the 3 most expensive store_products, highest price first.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,price FROM store_products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3

challenges.prompt: Show name and price of the 2 cheapest store_products, lowest price first.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,price FROM store_products ORDER BY price ASC LIMIT 2

lessons.title: Unique values with DISTINCT
lessons.reason: City NULL versus category values reinforces distinctness on two small columns.
lessons.concept: DISTINCT removes duplicate output rows. It applies to the whole set of selected columns, not just the first column. NULL is kept once.
lessons.example:
SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM store_customers;

walkthrough.title: See duplicate cities first
walkthrough.description: Many store_customers share a city. The raw list repeats Chicago and Austin. DISTINCT will keep one row per distinct value.
walkthrough.query: SELECT city FROM store_customers ORDER BY city;

walkthrough.title: Keep each city once
walkthrough.description: DISTINCT removes duplicate output rows across the selected columns. NULL is kept once if it appears.
walkthrough.query: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM store_customers;

hints: Add DISTINCT directly after SELECT.
Select just the column whose unique values you want.

quiz.q: What does SELECT DISTINCT city return?
options: One row for each different city value
quiz.why: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows. Repeated NULL values also appear only once.

challenges.prompt: Show each distinct customer city, including NULL.
challenges.answer: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM store_customers

challenges.prompt: Show each distinct product category.
challenges.answer: SELECT DISTINCT category FROM store_products

lessons.title: COUNT, SUM & AVG
lessons.reason: Row count transfers to quantity sum; quiz separates COUNT(*) from COUNT(nullable_column).
lessons.concept: Aggregate functions collapse rows into a summary. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) excludes NULL. SUM adds numeric values; AVG finds their mean.
lessons.example:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM store_customers;

walkthrough.title: Look at the rows being counted
walkthrough.description: Each customer is one row. An aggregate without GROUP BY collapses the whole table into one summary.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, name FROM store_customers;

walkthrough.title: Collapse to a single count
walkthrough.description: COUNT(*) counts rows. SUM and AVG work the same way: many input rows become one summary value.
walkthrough.query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count FROM store_customers;

hints: An aggregate query without GROUP BY returns one summary row.
Use COUNT(*) for rows or SUM(quantity) for units.

quiz.q: A table has three rows, and one city is NULL. What do COUNT(*) and COUNT(city) return?
quiz.why: COUNT(*) counts every row. COUNT(city) counts only rows with a non-NULL city.

challenges.prompt: Return the number of store_customers as customer_count.
challenges.answer: SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count FROM store_customers

challenges.prompt: Return total order quantity as total_units.
challenges.answer: SELECT SUM(quantity) AS total_units FROM store_orders

lessons.title: Group into summaries
lessons.reason: Category counts transfer to status totals; both explicitly change the result grain.
lessons.concept: GROUP BY forms one group for each key. Aggregates then summarize each group. Select grouping columns and aggregates to avoid ambiguous output.
lessons.example:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count
FROM store_products GROUP BY category;

walkthrough.title: Read product rows
walkthrough.description: Two store_products belong to each category. The input grain is one product.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,name,category FROM store_products;

walkthrough.title: Count within groups
walkthrough.description: GROUP BY changes the grain to one category.
walkthrough.query: SELECT category,COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM store_products GROUP BY category;

hints: Put the grouping key after GROUP BY.
Use COUNT(*) or SUM(quantity) for the summary column.

quiz.q: Products belong to two categories. What is the grain after GROUP BY category?
options: Always one row for the whole table
quiz.why: GROUP BY forms one group per category. Each output row summarizes that category.

challenges.prompt: Show category and product_count for each product category.
challenges.answer: SELECT category,COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM store_products GROUP BY category

challenges.prompt: Show status and total_units (sum of quantity) for each order status.
challenges.answer: SELECT status,SUM(quantity) AS total_units FROM store_orders GROUP BY status

lessons.title: MIN, MAX & the grain of a result
lessons.reason: Global MIN/MAX transfers to grouped maxima; quiz checks the one-row global summary grain.
lessons.concept: MIN and MAX summarize the smallest and largest values. The grain describes what one output row means. Adding GROUP BY changes that grain from one overall row to one row per group.
lessons.example:
SELECT MIN(watch_seconds) AS shortest_watch,
MAX(watch_seconds) AS longest_watch FROM watch_events;

walkthrough.title: Scan the watch lengths
walkthrough.description: Each event has watch_seconds. One overall MIN/MAX summarizes the whole table; GROUP BY later changes the grain.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, video_id, watch_seconds FROM watch_events ORDER BY id LIMIT 10;

walkthrough.title: Summarize at the overall grain
walkthrough.description: Without GROUP BY, MIN and MAX return one row for the entire result. That grain is “the whole table.”
walkthrough.query: SELECT MIN(watch_seconds) AS shortest_watch, MAX(watch_seconds) AS longest_watch FROM watch_events;

hints: Decide whether the task wants one overall row or one row per video.
Use MIN and MAX; put video_id in GROUP BY for the second task.

quiz.q: What is the grain of SELECT MIN(price), MAX(price) FROM products without GROUP BY?
options: One summary row for the whole input
quiz.why: Aggregates without GROUP BY summarize the input into one row. MIN and MAX find the lowest and highest values.

challenges.prompt: Return shortest_watch and longest_watch: minimum and maximum watch_seconds across all watch events.
challenges.answer: SELECT MIN(watch_seconds) AS shortest_watch,MAX(watch_seconds) AS longest_watch FROM watch_events

challenges.prompt: Return video_id and longest_watch: maximum watch_seconds for each video that has events.
challenges.answer: SELECT video_id,MAX(watch_seconds) AS longest_watch FROM watch_events GROUP BY video_id

lessons.title: Filter groups with HAVING
lessons.reason: Count-based HAVING transfers to a quantity threshold; filtering groups is the common concept.
lessons.concept: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Think rows → groups → group filter → output.

walkthrough.title: Form groups first
walkthrough.description: GROUP BY customer_id builds one row per customer with an order_count. HAVING will filter these groups next.
walkthrough.query: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM store_orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

walkthrough.title: Keep only qualifying groups
walkthrough.description: HAVING runs after aggregation. It removes groups whose aggregate fails the test, unlike WHERE which filters source rows.
walkthrough.query: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM store_orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

hints: Filter the aggregate in HAVING.
The aggregate expression must match the summary you are testing.

quiz.q: Which clause keeps only groups whose total quantity is greater than 10?
quiz.why: HAVING filters after aggregates are calculated. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.

challenges.prompt: Show customer_id and order_count for store_customers with at least 2 store_orders.
challenges.answer: SELECT customer_id,COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM store_orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*)>=2

challenges.prompt: Show customer_id and total_units for store_customers with total quantity greater than 3.
challenges.answer: SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS total_units FROM store_orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(quantity)>3

lessons.title: Make decisions with CASE
lessons.reason: Text classification transfers to a numeric indicator; ELSE and equality boundaries are explicit.
lessons.concept: CASE creates a value based on conditions. SQL checks WHEN branches in order and uses the first match. ELSE covers remaining rows.

walkthrough.title: Read the prices you will classify
walkthrough.description: Each product has a price. CASE will label rows at or above 80 as Premium and the rest as Standard.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, price FROM store_products ORDER BY price;

walkthrough.title: Assign a tier with CASE
walkthrough.description: WHEN branches are checked in order. The first true branch wins; ELSE covers everything else.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, CASE WHEN price >= 80 THEN 'Premium' ELSE 'Standard' END AS tier FROM store_products;

hints: CASE WHEN condition THEN value ELSE value END.
Add AS tier or AS is_paid.

quiz.q: If no WHEN condition matches a CASE expression, what does ELSE supply?
options: A filter that removes the row
quiz.why: CASE chooses a value for each row. ELSE is the fallback when no WHEN condition is true.

challenges.prompt: Show name and tier: Premium if price >= 80, otherwise Standard.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,CASE WHEN price>=80 THEN 'Premium' ELSE 'Standard' END AS tier FROM store_products

challenges.prompt: Show id and is_paid: 1 for paid store_orders, otherwise 0.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_paid FROM store_orders

lessons.title: Conditional aggregation
lessons.reason: Weather count transfers to conditional Celsius averaging; missing/flagged values must not become zero.
lessons.concept: Conditional aggregation measures selected rows while keeping the group. SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts matches. AVG(CASE WHEN condition THEN value END) averages matching non-NULL values. The missing ELSE produces NULL, which AVG ignores; ELSE 0 would change the denominator. In weather data, a missing observation is not a zero temperature.
lessons.example: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN element='PRCP' AND raw_value>0 AND quality_flag IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS wet_observations FROM daily_weather;

walkthrough.title: Inspect the measurement grain
walkthrough.description: Each station-date has separate rows for different measurement elements. Values have element-specific units.
walkthrough.query: SELECT station_id,date,element,raw_value,quality_flag FROM daily_weather WHERE date='2024-01-01' ORDER BY station_id,element;

walkthrough.title: Count only qualifying observations
walkthrough.description: The CASE contributes one for an unflagged positive precipitation value and zero otherwise.
walkthrough.query: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN element='PRCP' AND raw_value>0 AND quality_flag IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS wet_observations FROM daily_weather;

hints: Put the element and quality conditions inside CASE.
For an average, omit ELSE so unmatched or missing values do not become zero.

quiz.q: What does SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) count?
quiz.why: Each paid row contributes one; other rows contribute zero. The aggregate adds those contributions.

challenges.prompt: Return wet_observations: the number of daily_weather rows with element PRCP, raw_value greater than zero and no quality_flag. A missing value does not count as wet.
challenges.answer: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN element='PRCP' AND raw_value>0 AND quality_flag IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS wet_observations FROM daily_weather

challenges.prompt: For every station_id present in daily_weather, return station_id and avg_tmax_c: the average usable TMAX in Celsius, rounded to two decimals. A usable value has quality_flag NULL and raw_value non-NULL. Divide raw tenths by 10.0. Preserve NULL if no usable TMAX exists; do not average other elements as zeros.
challenges.answer: SELECT station_id,ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN element='TMAX' AND quality_flag IS NULL THEN raw_value/10.0 END),2) AS avg_tmax_c FROM daily_weather GROUP BY station_id

lessons.title: CAST & numeric measurements
lessons.reason: Sensor CAST transfers to numeric deviation with Celsius units; quiz now warns that coercion is not validation.
lessons.concept: CAST changes a value’s representation; arithmetic and rounding operate on numeric measurements. Keep the measurement’s units explicit. Casting text to a number is not a general data-validation rule in SQLite.
lessons.example: SELECT device_id,observed_at,temperature_c,CAST(temperature_c AS TEXT) AS as_text FROM sensor_readings WHERE device_id=1 LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One device-time reading.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM sensor_readings LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT device_id,observed_at,temperature_c,CAST(temperature_c AS TEXT) AS as_text FROM sensor_readings WHERE device_id=1 LIMIT 5

hints: CAST temperature_c AS TEXT for the first task.
Calculate ABS(temperature_c-20.0), then ROUND to two decimals.

quiz.q: Does CAST(raw_text AS REAL) prove a text value was a valid measurement?
options: Yes, every numeric result is validated
No, SQLite can coerce invalid text to zero
quiz.why: Conversion changes representation; validation requires separate rules for the accepted source format.

challenges.prompt: Return device_id, observed_at and temperature_text by casting temperature_c to TEXT for every sensor reading.
challenges.answer: SELECT device_id,observed_at,CAST(temperature_c AS TEXT) AS temperature_text FROM sensor_readings

challenges.prompt: Return device_id, observed_at and deviation_c: absolute difference between temperature_c and 20.0 Celsius, rounded to two decimals.
challenges.answer: SELECT device_id,observed_at,ROUND(ABS(temperature_c-20.0),2) AS deviation_c FROM sensor_readings

lessons.title: Databases, schemas, tables & keys
lessons.reason: Schema inspection transfers to a real key-based join; canonical table names now agree with sqlite_schema.
lessons.concept: SQL is the language; the database engine executes it. Tables contain rows and typed columns. A primary key identifies one row; a foreign key points to another table — for example, store_orders.customer_id points at store_customers.id. To read columns from both tables in one result, match those keys with JOIN: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer_name FROM store_orders o JOIN store_customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id. The next lesson practices joins in depth; here you use the pattern once so the key relationship is concrete. SQLite catalogs differ from SQL Server schemas. In this app each worker creates an in-memory SQLite database.
lessons.example:
SELECT name,type FROM sqlite_schema
WHERE type='table' AND name IN('store_customers','store_products','store_orders');

walkthrough.title: Find the tables and their keys
walkthrough.description: sqlite_schema lists table names. In this shop database, store_customers.id is a primary key and store_orders.customer_id is the foreign key that points to it.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT name, type FROM sqlite_schema
WHERE type = 'table' AND name IN ('store_customers', 'store_products', 'store_orders');

walkthrough.title: Match related rows with JOIN
walkthrough.description: JOIN pairs each order with the customer whose id equals store_orders.customer_id. That is how a foreign key becomes a readable result. Challenge 2 asks for this shape.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer_name
FROM store_orders o
JOIN store_customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
LIMIT 8;

hints: Metadata describes the database objects. sqlite_schema lists tables.
For challenge 2, JOIN store_orders to store_customers on store_orders.customer_id = store_customers.id and alias the columns order_id and customer_name.

quiz.q: What does a foreign key describe?
options: A relationship from a column to a key in another table
A name for every numeric column
quiz.why: A foreign key links records to a referenced key. With enforcement enabled, an invalid reference is rejected.

challenges.prompt: Return name and type for the store_customers, store_products and store_orders tables from sqlite_schema.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,type FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='table' AND name IN('store_customers','store_products','store_orders')

challenges.prompt: Return order_id and customer_name by joining store_orders.customer_id to store_customers.id for every order.
challenges.answer: SELECT o.id AS order_id,c.name AS customer_name FROM store_orders o JOIN store_customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id

lessons.title: Connect tables with JOIN
lessons.reason: Two foreign-key joins intentionally reinforce relationship direction before outer joins.
lessons.concept: INNER JOIN pairs rows whose join condition matches. Aliases keep column references short. One customer can match several store_orders, so joins can increase row counts.
lessons.example:
SELECT o.id, c.name FROM store_orders o
JOIN store_customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;

walkthrough.title: Find the matching keys
walkthrough.description: store_orders.customer_id references store_customers.id. Read both columns so the JOIN condition is concrete before you write it.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id AS order_id, customer_id FROM store_orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 8;

walkthrough.title: Combine matching rows with JOIN
walkthrough.description: INNER JOIN keeps only pairs that satisfy the ON condition. Aliases keep the two id columns clear.
walkthrough.query: SELECT o.id, c.name FROM store_orders o JOIN store_customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;

hints: Match the foreign key in store_orders to the other table's id.
Use table aliases to distinguish the two id columns.

quiz.q: What does an INNER JOIN do with a customer who has no matching order?
options: Keeps the customer with NULL order columns
Leaves the customer out of the joined result
Invents an order for the customer
quiz.why: INNER JOIN returns matching pairs only. A customer with several matching store_orders appears once for each match.

challenges.prompt: Return every order id and its customer name (columns id, name).
challenges.answer: SELECT o.id,c.name FROM store_orders o JOIN store_customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id

challenges.prompt: Return every order id and its product name (columns id, name).
challenges.answer: SELECT o.id,p.name FROM store_orders o JOIN store_products p ON p.id=o.product_id

lessons.title: Keep unmatched rows
lessons.reason: Preserving all customers transfers to selecting only unmatched customers; COUNT(key) is essential.
lessons.concept: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table. When no match exists, right-side columns are NULL. A right-table filter in WHERE may remove those unmatched rows.

walkthrough.title: Identify the preserved side
walkthrough.description: Every customer must stay, even Hugo without an order.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM store_customers;

walkthrough.title: Inspect the joined rows
walkthrough.description: Customers repeat for each order. Hugo gets a NULL right-side id.
walkthrough.query: SELECT c.id,c.name,o.id AS order_id FROM store_customers c LEFT JOIN store_orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id;

walkthrough.title: Count matching right-side ids
walkthrough.description: COUNT(o.id) ignores the unmatched NULL and gives Hugo zero.
walkthrough.query: SELECT c.name,COUNT(o.id) AS order_count FROM store_customers c LEFT JOIN store_orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id GROUP BY c.id,c.name;

hints: Customers must be on the left side.
COUNT(o.id) ignores NULL; COUNT(*) would count the unmatched placeholder row.

quiz.q: After a LEFT JOIN, how do you count zero store_orders for a customer with no match?
quiz.why: The customer row is preserved, but o.id is NULL. COUNT(o.id) ignores that NULL and returns zero.

challenges.prompt: Show every customer name and order_count, including store_customers with zero store_orders.
challenges.answer: SELECT c.name,COUNT(o.id) AS order_count FROM store_customers c LEFT JOIN store_orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id GROUP BY c.id,c.name

challenges.prompt: Show name for store_customers with no store_orders.
challenges.answer: SELECT c.name FROM store_customers c LEFT JOIN store_orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL

lessons.title: Ratios, ROUND & NULLIF
lessons.reason: Observed-account rates transfer to the full account population; no-request denominators remain NULL.
lessons.concept: A rate is numerator divided by denominator. Use a real number (100.0) to avoid integer division. NULLIF(x,0) turns a zero denominator into NULL; ROUND controls displayed precision. Preserve that NULL instead of calling an undefined rate zero.

walkthrough.title: Count successes and attempts
walkthrough.description: A success rate needs both numerator and denominator. NULLIF protects against dividing by zero.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT account_id,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS successes,
  COUNT(*) AS attempts
FROM ai_requests GROUP BY account_id;

walkthrough.title: Turn counts into a rounded percent
walkthrough.description: Multiply by 100.0 for a real division, wrap the denominator in NULLIF(..., 0), then ROUND to two decimals.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT account_id, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 2) AS success_pct
FROM ai_requests GROUP BY account_id;

hints: Count requests, not placeholder rows produced by LEFT JOIN.
Use 100.0 * successes / NULLIF(COUNT(r.id),0) for all accounts.

quiz.q: What does NULLIF(denominator, 0) do when the denominator is zero?
options: Returns NULL so a ratio can represent an undefined result
quiz.why: NULLIF returns NULL when its arguments are equal. Division by that missing denominator produces NULL rather than a meaningful ratio.

challenges.prompt: Return account_id and success_pct (0–100, rounded to 2 decimals) for accounts with requests.
challenges.answer: SELECT account_id,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN status='success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(COUNT(*),0),2) AS success_pct FROM ai_requests GROUP BY account_id

challenges.prompt: Return id and success_pct for every account, including accounts with no requests (NULL rate). Round to 2 decimals.
challenges.answer: SELECT a.id,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN r.status='success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(COUNT(r.id),0),2) AS success_pct FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN ai_requests r ON r.account_id=a.id GROUP BY a.id

lessons.title: Revenue across tables
lessons.reason: Customer revenue transfers to category revenue; purchase-line grain is stated and price multiplication precedes aggregation.
lessons.concept: Join transaction rows to product prices, multiply price by quantity, then aggregate at the desired grain. Filter status before computing paid revenue.
lessons.example:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS revenue
FROM store_orders o JOIN store_customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id
JOIN store_products p ON p.id=o.product_id
WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id,c.name;

walkthrough.title: Read an order line with its price
walkthrough.description: Join one order line to its product so quantity and price sit on the same row. The next step multiplies them and aggregates paid revenue.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT o.id, o.quantity, p.price, o.status
FROM store_orders o
JOIN store_products p ON p.id = o.product_id
LIMIT 8;

walkthrough.title: Run the reference
walkthrough.description: Join transaction rows to product prices, multiply price by quantity, then aggregate at the desired grain. Filter status before computing paid revenue.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS revenue
FROM store_orders o JOIN store_customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id
JOIN store_products p ON p.id=o.product_id
WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id,c.name;

hints: Revenue per order is quantity * price.
Join store_products on product_id and filter to paid before grouping.

quiz.q: What does quantity * price compute for one paid order line?
options: The customer's lifetime value across all store_orders
That line's revenue before you aggregate by customer or category
The number of store_products in the order
quiz.why: Each order row is one product line. Multiplying quantity by price gives that line's revenue; SUM and GROUP BY then produce a total at the grain you choose.

challenges.prompt: Show customer name and paid revenue (alias revenue), only store_customers with paid store_orders.
challenges.answer: SELECT c.name,SUM(o.quantity*p.price) AS revenue FROM store_orders o JOIN store_customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN store_products p ON p.id=o.product_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id,c.name

challenges.prompt: Show category and paid revenue (alias revenue) for each category with paid store_orders.
challenges.answer: SELECT p.category,SUM(o.quantity*p.price) AS revenue FROM store_orders o JOIN store_products p ON p.id=o.product_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY p.category

lessons.title: Self-joins & manager relationships
lessons.reason: Developer manager roles replace referral labels; transfer compares employee and direct-manager salaries after joining.
lessons.concept: A self join connects different roles in the same table. Here an employee row references another employee as its manager. Use aliases to distinguish the two roles, and choose LEFT JOIN when people without managers must remain.
lessons.example: SELECT e.name AS employee,m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id=e.manager_id WHERE e.id<=5

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One employee and at most one direct manager.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM employees LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT e.name AS employee,m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id=e.manager_id WHERE e.id<=5

hints: Use employees twice, with separate aliases for employee and manager.
Compare salaries only after joining the direct manager; a missing manager cannot satisfy a greater-than comparison.

quiz.q: Why use two aliases for employees in a manager join?
options: The aliases create two copies of the data
Each alias names a different role in the relationship
quiz.why: The employee and manager are rows from the same table. Aliases distinguish their keys and attributes.

challenges.prompt: Return employee_id and manager_name for every employee, preserving NULL manager_name when manager_id has no match.
challenges.answer: SELECT e.id AS employee_id,m.name AS manager_name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id=e.manager_id

challenges.prompt: Return employee_id and manager_id for employees whose salary is greater than their direct manager’s salary. Exclude employees without a manager.
challenges.answer: SELECT e.id AS employee_id,m.id AS manager_id FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id=e.manager_id WHERE e.salary>m.salary

lessons.title: CROSS JOIN & a complete date grid
lessons.reason: A provided date list teaches Cartesian grids before recursion; challenge 2 adds signup eligibility and stays lesson-only.
lessons.concept: CROSS JOIN creates every pair of rows. It is useful for a deliberate date × entity grid, but careless use multiplies data. The three dates below are supplied setup data via a VALUES list—you are not being tested on UNION. Focus on CROSS JOIN (and optional signup filtering).

walkthrough.title: Use the provided three dates
walkthrough.description: These three day values are setup data (a VALUES list). You do not need UNION or recursion—your job is the CROSS JOIN next.

walkthrough.title: Pair every date with every viewer
walkthrough.description: CROSS JOIN multiplies the date list by the viewers. Filter by signup_at only after the grid exists when the task asks for that.

hints: Treat the VALUES date list as given setup data, then CROSS JOIN viewers.
Filter day >= signup_at after creating the grid for the second task.

quiz.q: How many combinations does a CROSS JOIN of two customers and three dates produce?
quiz.why: A CROSS JOIN pairs every row on one side with every row on the other: two times three combinations.

challenges.prompt: Return day and viewer_id for every day from 2025-01-01 through 2025-01-03 inclusive and every viewer, including pre-signup combinations.
challenges.answer: SELECT day,v.id AS viewer_id FROM (SELECT column1 AS day FROM (VALUES ('2025-01-01'), ('2025-01-02'), ('2025-01-03'))) AS days CROSS JOIN viewers v

challenges.prompt: Return day and viewer_id for the same date range, keeping only combinations on or after that viewer's signup_at.
challenges.answer: SELECT day,v.id AS viewer_id FROM (SELECT column1 AS day FROM (VALUES ('2025-01-01'), ('2025-01-02'), ('2025-01-03'))) AS days CROSS JOIN viewers v WHERE day>=v.signup_at

lessons.title: FULL OUTER JOIN & unmatched records
lessons.reason: Matched and unmatched invoice/payment rows transfer to orphan detection; split payments remain separate rows.
lessons.concept: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides. Reconciliation often needs this to find missing records. This SQLite version supports FULL OUTER JOIN; older SQLite versions did not.
lessons.example:
SELECT i.id AS invoice_id,p.id AS payment_id
FROM invoices i FULL OUTER JOIN invoice_payments p ON p.invoice_id=i.id;

walkthrough.title: See invoice and payment keys
walkthrough.description: Some invoices lack invoice_payments and some invoice_payments lack invoices. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides.

walkthrough.title: Retain unmatched rows on both sides
walkthrough.description: FULL OUTER JOIN returns matches plus leftovers from either table. Missing matches show NULL on the empty side.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT i.id AS invoice_id, p.id AS payment_id
FROM invoices i FULL OUTER JOIN invoice_payments p ON p.invoice_id = i.id;

hints: Use FULL OUTER JOIN for retaining both sides.
A missing invoice match has i.id IS NULL.

quiz.q: Which unmatched rows does a FULL OUTER JOIN preserve?
options: Only unmatched rows on the left
Only unmatched rows on the right
quiz.why: A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps matching pairs and unmatched rows from either side, filling the other side with NULL.

challenges.prompt: Return invoice_id and payment_id for every invoice/payment match, retaining unmatched rows on either side. Keep split invoice_payments as separate rows.
challenges.answer: SELECT i.id AS invoice_id,p.id AS payment_id FROM invoices i FULL OUTER JOIN invoice_payments p ON p.invoice_id=i.id

challenges.prompt: Return payment_id for invoice_payments whose invoice_id has no matching invoice, including NULL invoice_id.
challenges.answer: SELECT p.id AS payment_id FROM invoice_payments p LEFT JOIN invoices i ON i.id=p.invoice_id WHERE i.id IS NULL

lessons.title: ON versus WHERE in a LEFT JOIN
lessons.reason: Healthcare provider counts transfer to the registered-patient denominator; ON filtering and COUNT(key) preserve zero groups.
lessons.concept: A condition in LEFT JOIN ON limits matching right-side rows while retaining the left-side population. The same condition in WHERE can discard the NULL-extended rows. Count the matched encounter key to report zero accurately.
lessons.example: SELECT p.id,e.id AS encounter_id FROM providers p LEFT JOIN encounters e ON e.provider_id=p.id AND e.status='cancelled' WHERE p.id<=3

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One provider in the first task; one registered patient in the second.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM providers LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT p.id,e.id AS encounter_id FROM providers p LEFT JOIN encounters e ON e.provider_id=p.id AND e.status='cancelled' WHERE p.id<=3

hints: Keep the completed condition inside ON.
Start from patients for a patient denominator, then count the joined encounter id.

quiz.q: Where should a completed-encounter condition go to retain every provider in a LEFT JOIN?
options: In ON, so unmatched providers remain
Only in WHERE, to remove unmatched providers
quiz.why: Filtering matches in ON preserves the left-side population. A WHERE condition requiring a right-side value removes unmatched rows.

challenges.prompt: Return provider_id and completed_visits for every provider. Include zero for providers with no completed encounter.
challenges.answer: SELECT p.id AS provider_id,COUNT(e.id) AS completed_visits FROM providers p LEFT JOIN encounters e ON e.provider_id=p.id AND e.status='completed' GROUP BY p.id

challenges.prompt: Return patient_id and cancelled_visits for every patient. Count only cancelled encounters, retaining patients with no cancelled encounters as zero.
challenges.answer: SELECT p.id AS patient_id,COUNT(e.id) AS cancelled_visits FROM patients p LEFT JOIN encounters e ON e.patient_id=p.id AND e.status='cancelled' GROUP BY p.id

lessons.title: Combine sets with UNION
lessons.reason: UNION versus UNION ALL intentionally contrast set and bag behavior; duplicates are the transfer edge case.
lessons.concept: UNION stacks compatible query outputs and removes duplicate rows. UNION ALL retains duplicates. Both sides need the same number of columns in matching positions.
lessons.example:
SELECT city FROM store_customers WHERE city='Chicago'
UNION SELECT city FROM store_customers WHERE city='Austin';

walkthrough.title: Build two compatible city lists
walkthrough.description: Chicago and Austin rows each produce a city column. UNION stacks compatible selects and drops duplicates.
walkthrough.query: SELECT city FROM store_customers WHERE city IN ('Chicago', 'Austin') ORDER BY city;

walkthrough.title: Stack sets with UNION
walkthrough.description: UNION removes duplicates across the stacked rows. UNION ALL would keep every duplicate.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT city FROM store_customers WHERE city = 'Chicago'
UNION SELECT city FROM store_customers WHERE city = 'Austin';

hints: Stack SELECT statements using UNION or UNION ALL.
The output column name comes from the first SELECT.

quiz.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
options: UNION removes duplicate result rows; UNION ALL keeps them
UNION ALL sorts the rows automatically
UNION combines columns instead of rows
quiz.why: Both combine compatible result rows. UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL preserves them.

challenges.prompt: Return distinct city values from Chicago store_customers and Austin store_customers using UNION.
challenges.answer: SELECT city FROM store_customers WHERE city='Chicago' UNION SELECT city FROM store_customers WHERE city='Austin'

challenges.prompt: Stack name from store_customers and name from store_products, keeping duplicates.
challenges.answer: SELECT name FROM store_customers UNION ALL SELECT name FROM store_products

lessons.title: INTERSECT & EXCEPT
lessons.reason: INTERSECT and EXCEPT contrast shared membership with one-sided exclusion; each output is distinct.
lessons.concept: INTERSECT keeps distinct rows appearing in both results. EXCEPT keeps distinct rows from the first result that are absent from the second. Column positions and types should align.
lessons.example:
SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=1
INTERSECT SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=2;

walkthrough.title: List viewers of video 1
walkthrough.description: INTERSECT will keep viewers who also watched video 2. EXCEPT would keep viewers of video 1 who never watched video 2.
walkthrough.query: SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id = 1 ORDER BY viewer_id;

walkthrough.title: Keep viewers in both sets
walkthrough.description: INTERSECT returns distinct rows present in both SELECT results. Column positions must align.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id = 1
INTERSECT SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id = 2;

hints: Build one set of viewer ids for each video.
INTERSECT is both; EXCEPT is first minus second.

quiz.q: What does A EXCEPT B return?
options: Distinct rows in A that are absent from B
quiz.why: EXCEPT subtracts the right result from the left and returns distinct remaining rows.

challenges.prompt: Return viewer_id for viewers who watched both video 1 and video 2. Each viewer appears once.
challenges.answer: SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=1 INTERSECT SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=2

challenges.prompt: Return viewer_id for viewers who watched video 1 but never video 2. Each viewer appears once.
challenges.answer: SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=1 EXCEPT SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=2

lessons.title: Subqueries
lessons.reason: Replaces a second overall average with an own-category correlated benchmark; explanation and quiz now teach correlation.
lessons.concept: A scalar subquery supplies one value to the outer query. An uncorrelated average compares every product with the same benchmark. A correlated subquery can calculate a different benchmark for each product category.
lessons.example: SELECT category,AVG(price) AS benchmark FROM store_products GROUP BY category

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One product whose price exceeds the requested benchmark.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM store_products LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT category,AVG(price) AS benchmark FROM store_products GROUP BY category

hints: Calculate the overall AVG(price) in a subquery first.
For a category benchmark, match the inner category to the outer product category.

quiz.q: What changes when the subquery compares its category with the outer product category?
options: Every product is still compared with one overall average
The benchmark depends on the outer product category
The outer query returns one row per category
quiz.why: The correlation limits the inner rows separately for each outer product. The output still has product grain.

challenges.prompt: Return name and price for store_products priced above the overall average product price.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,price FROM store_products WHERE price>(SELECT AVG(price) FROM store_products)

challenges.prompt: Return name and price for store_products priced above the average price in their own category. A product equal to its category average does not qualify.
challenges.answer: SELECT p.name,p.price FROM store_products p WHERE p.price>(SELECT AVG(x.price) FROM store_products x WHERE x.category=p.category)

lessons.title: Ask whether a row exists
lessons.reason: EXISTS versus NOT EXISTS intentionally contrast positive and negative quantification without fan-out.
lessons.concept: EXISTS is true when its subquery returns at least one row. A correlated subquery refers to the outer row. NOT EXISTS is useful for finding missing relationships.

walkthrough.title: Check for a matching paid order
walkthrough.description: EXISTS asks whether at least one related row satisfies the inner filter. It does not multiply the outer customer rows.
walkthrough.query: SELECT c.id, c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.status FROM store_customers c LEFT JOIN store_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY c.id LIMIT 12;

walkthrough.title: Keep store_customers with a match
walkthrough.description: EXISTS returns true when the correlated subquery finds one or more rows. The outer SELECT lists those store_customers once.
walkthrough.query: SELECT c.name FROM store_customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM store_orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid');

hints: Correlate customer_id to the outer customer id.
Use EXISTS for at least one, NOT EXISTS for none.

quiz.q: What does NOT EXISTS test for each outer row?
options: Whether the subquery finds no matching rows
Whether every selected value is NULL
Whether the outer table is empty
quiz.why: NOT EXISTS is true when the correlated subquery returns no rows. It tests existence, not the value selected.

challenges.prompt: Show name of store_customers who have at least one paid order.
challenges.answer: SELECT c.name FROM store_customers c WHERE EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM store_orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid')

challenges.prompt: Show name of store_customers who have no paid store_orders.
challenges.answer: SELECT c.name FROM store_customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM store_orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid')

lessons.title: NOT IN and the NULL trap
lessons.reason: Nullable anti-membership transfers to a known-country exclusion; lesson makes UNKNOWN explicit.
lessons.concept: NOT reverses true and false, but unknown stays unknown. If a NOT IN list contains NULL, a nonmatching comparison can become unknown and disappear from WHERE. Prefer NOT EXISTS for nullable relationships.

walkthrough.title: Inspect nullable relationships
walkthrough.description: NULL here means no referring viewer.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,referred_by FROM viewers;

walkthrough.title: See the NOT IN trap
walkthrough.description: A NULL in this subquery makes NOT IN unknown for nonmatches. Observe the empty result.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id FROM viewers WHERE id NOT IN(SELECT referred_by FROM viewers);

walkthrough.title: Use an existence test
walkthrough.description: NOT EXISTS asks whether a matching referring relationship is absent.
walkthrough.query: SELECT v.id FROM viewers v WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM viewers r WHERE r.referred_by=v.id);

hints: The nullable referred_by column makes a bare NOT IN unsafe.
Correlate the inner referred_by to the outer viewer id with NOT EXISTS.

quiz.q: Why can NOT IN (SELECT nullable_key ...) unexpectedly return no rows?
options: NULL can turn nonmatching comparisons into unknown
quiz.why: Unknown does not pass WHERE. Filter NULLs from the list or use NOT EXISTS.

challenges.prompt: Return id for viewers who have not referred anyone. A referred_by value identifies the referrer, and NULL means no referrer.
challenges.answer: SELECT v.id FROM viewers v WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM viewers r WHERE r.referred_by=v.id)

challenges.prompt: Return id and country for viewers outside US and GB.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,country FROM viewers WHERE country NOT IN('US','GB')

lessons.title: Readable queries with CTEs
lessons.reason: Two named aggregate CTEs reinforce decomposition before windows; no unnecessary staging tables.
lessons.concept: WITH names a temporary query result for this statement. Common table expressions help you separate a complicated question into understandable stages. They do not create permanent tables.

walkthrough.title: Name an intermediate total
walkthrough.description: WITH defines a temporary result you can read like a table. Here each customer gets a units total before filtering.
walkthrough.query: SELECT customer_id, SUM(quantity) AS units FROM store_orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

walkthrough.title: Filter the named CTE
walkthrough.description: The outer query reads totals as if it were a table. CTEs make multi-step logic easier to follow than nested subqueries.

hints: Define the intermediate result with WITH name AS (...).
The outer query filters the named result.

quiz.q: What does WITH totals AS (...) create?
options: A permanent table saved for later queries
A named query result available within this statement
An index on the source table
quiz.why: A common table expression names a query result for the current statement. It does not create a permanent table.

challenges.prompt: Use a CTE to return customer_id and units for store_customers whose total quantity exceeds 3.
challenges.answer: WITH totals AS(SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM store_orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT customer_id,units FROM totals WHERE units>3

challenges.prompt: Use a CTE to return category and avg_price for categories with average price greater than 30.
challenges.answer: WITH averages AS(SELECT category,AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM store_products GROUP BY category) SELECT category,avg_price FROM averages WHERE avg_price>30

lessons.title: Dates & monthly analysis
lessons.reason: Mobility pickup-month trip counts transfer to card meter-fare totals; pickup time, cents and tips are distinguished.
lessons.concept: ISO timestamps can be bucketed into months with substr(timestamp,1,7). Choose which event timestamp defines the reporting period. A trip that crosses midnight belongs to different calendar dates depending on whether you use pickup or dropoff.
lessons.example: SELECT substr(picked_up_at,1,13) AS pickup_hour,COUNT(*) AS trips FROM trips GROUP BY pickup_hour

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One month summary of completed trips, using pickup time.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM trips LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT substr(picked_up_at,1,13) AS pickup_hour,COUNT(*) AS trips FROM trips GROUP BY pickup_hour

hints: Group substr(picked_up_at,1,7).
Sum fare_cents in integer cents; do not join zones or add tip_cents for this task.

quiz.q: What does grouping substr(picked_up_at,1,7) produce for ISO timestamps?
options: One row per calendar year and month
One row per month name across all years
quiz.why: The prefix retains both year and month, so January in different years remains in separate groups.

challenges.prompt: Return month (YYYY-MM) and trip_count for every observed pickup month in trips.
challenges.answer: SELECT substr(picked_up_at,1,7) AS month,COUNT(*) AS trip_count FROM trips GROUP BY month

challenges.prompt: Return month (YYYY-MM) and fare_cents for pickup months. Sum meter fare_cents only for card payments (payment_type=1); exclude tips.
challenges.answer: SELECT substr(picked_up_at,1,7) AS month,SUM(fare_cents) AS fare_cents FROM trips WHERE payment_type=1 GROUP BY month

lessons.title: Clean strings & cast values
lessons.reason: Normalization transfers to domain extraction; preserving NULL is explicit, and this is not general email validation.
lessons.concept: TRIM removes outside spaces, LOWER normalizes case, SUBSTR extracts a portion, and CAST makes a conversion explicit. Keep NULL visible when the source is missing. SQLite uses SUBSTR; many engines also provide SUBSTRING.
lessons.example: SELECT id,LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS clean_email FROM members;

walkthrough.title: See messy emails before cleaning
walkthrough.description: Whitespace and mixed case make the same address look different. Cleaning must happen before you compare or group.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, email FROM members ORDER BY id LIMIT 8;

walkthrough.title: Normalize with TRIM and LOWER
walkthrough.description: TRIM removes surrounding spaces; LOWER folds case. Together they produce a stable clean_email.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS clean_email FROM members;

hints: Nest LOWER around TRIM.
INSTR finds @; SUBSTR starts one character after it.

quiz.q: Why apply TRIM before comparing a text identifier?
options: To remove leading and trailing spaces
To remove every space inside the identifier
To convert all text to a number
quiz.why: TRIM removes surrounding spaces. It keeps internal spaces; case normalization and type conversion are separate operations.

challenges.prompt: Return id and clean_email for every member: trim outside spaces and lowercase the email; preserve NULL.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS clean_email FROM members

challenges.prompt: Return id and email_domain: lowercase, trim, and take the email text after @. Preserve NULL.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,SUBSTR(LOWER(TRIM(email)),INSTR(TRIM(email),'@')+1) AS email_domain FROM members

lessons.title: Date boundaries & monthly buckets
lessons.reason: Flight schedule boundaries use explicit UTC half-open intervals; transfer counts distinct scheduled aircraft by month.
lessons.concept: Use an inclusive start and exclusive end for timestamp periods. An end bound at midnight on the last day excludes most of that day. These flight timestamps use UTC; no local-time conversion is implied.
lessons.example: SELECT id,scheduled_departure FROM flights WHERE scheduled_departure>='2025-01-03T00:00:00Z' AND scheduled_departure<'2025-01-04T00:00:00Z'

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One scheduled flight in the first task; one observed schedule month in the second.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM flights LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,scheduled_departure FROM flights WHERE scheduled_departure>='2025-01-03T00:00:00Z' AND scheduled_departure<'2025-01-04T00:00:00Z'

hints: Use scheduled_departure >= start AND scheduled_departure < next month.
Count distinct aircraft_id within the month, not flight rows.

quiz.q: Which range includes every January timestamp and excludes February?
quiz.why: A half-open interval handles the full last day and excludes the next boundary.

challenges.prompt: Return id and scheduled_departure for flights scheduled in January 2025, including the full final day and excluding February.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,scheduled_departure FROM flights WHERE scheduled_departure>='2025-01-01T00:00:00Z' AND scheduled_departure<'2025-02-01T00:00:00Z'

challenges.prompt: Return month (YYYY-MM) and scheduled_aircraft: distinct aircraft_id values in each scheduled-departure month. Include cancelled flights.
challenges.answer: SELECT substr(scheduled_departure,1,7) AS month,COUNT(DISTINCT aircraft_id) AS scheduled_aircraft FROM flights GROUP BY month

lessons.title: Window functions: ROW_NUMBER
lessons.reason: Chronological row numbering transfers to partitioned price ordering with deterministic ties.
lessons.concept: Window functions calculate across related rows while keeping each row visible. ROW_NUMBER assigns 1, 2, 3 within a partition using its ORDER BY. Include a tie-breaker for repeatable results.

walkthrough.title: Order a customer's store_orders
walkthrough.description: ROW_NUMBER needs a clear order within each partition. Sort one customer's store_orders by time to see the sequence.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, customer_id, ordered_at FROM store_orders WHERE customer_id = 1 ORDER BY ordered_at, id;

walkthrough.title: Number rows inside each partition
walkthrough.description: PARTITION BY customer_id restarts the counter for each customer. ORDER BY decides which row is 1, 2, 3…

hints: PARTITION BY restarts numbering per group.
Put ORDER BY inside OVER to control numbering.

quiz.q: What does ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at, id) do?
options: Collapses each customer to one row
Numbers each customer’s rows from 1, keeping every row
Uses one numbering sequence for all store_customers
quiz.why: PARTITION BY starts a new sequence for each customer. ORDER BY sets the sequence; id breaks equal timestamps.

challenges.prompt: Return id, customer_id and order_number: number each customer's store_orders by ordered_at then id.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,customer_id,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at,id) AS order_number FROM store_orders

challenges.prompt: Return name, category and price_rank: number store_products within category by price descending then id.
challenges.answer: SELECT name,category,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS price_rank FROM store_products

lessons.title: RANK & DENSE_RANK
lessons.reason: Sports goal ranking includes unused players; transfer ranks within teams and distinguishes RANK from DENSE_RANK.
lessons.concept: RANK shares a position across equal values and leaves gaps after ties. DENSE_RANK shares ties without gaps. Aggregate at player grain before ranking player totals; include registered players without appearances when the task asks for every player.
lessons.example: SELECT game_id,player_id,minutes,RANK() OVER(ORDER BY minutes DESC) AS rank FROM appearances WHERE game_id=1

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One registered player, including players with no appearances.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM appearances LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT game_id,player_id,minutes,RANK() OVER(ORDER BY minutes DESC) AS rank FROM appearances WHERE game_id=1

hints: LEFT JOIN appearances and aggregate goals at player grain.
Partition by team_id for the second task; rank the total, not individual appearances.

quiz.q: For tied values 100, 100, 90, what do RANK and DENSE_RANK assign to 90?
quiz.why: RANK leaves a gap after a tie. DENSE_RANK counts distinct ranked values without gaps.

challenges.prompt: Return player_id, goals and rank for every player. goals is the total across appearances, zero with none. Use RANK by goals descending; equal totals share a rank.
challenges.answer: WITH totals AS (SELECT p.id AS player_id,COALESCE(SUM(a.goals),0) AS goals FROM players p LEFT JOIN appearances a ON a.player_id=p.id GROUP BY p.id) SELECT player_id,goals,RANK() OVER(ORDER BY goals DESC) AS rank FROM totals

challenges.prompt: Return player_id, team_id, goals and rank for every player. Rank total goals within the registered team using DENSE_RANK descending, with zero goals for players without appearances.
challenges.answer: WITH totals AS (SELECT p.id AS player_id,p.team_id,COALESCE(SUM(a.goals),0) AS goals FROM players p LEFT JOIN appearances a ON a.player_id=p.id GROUP BY p.id) SELECT player_id,team_id,goals,DENSE_RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY team_id ORDER BY goals DESC) AS rank FROM totals

lessons.title: Running totals
lessons.reason: Payments cumulative posted debits transfer from global to account partitions; explicitly excludes refunds and starting balance.
lessons.concept: A running total accumulates rows in an explicit order. ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW includes each posting exactly once. Partitioning restarts the accumulation for each account.
lessons.example: SELECT id,amount_cents,SUM(amount_cents) OVER(ORDER BY posted_at,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS total_cents FROM settlements WHERE id<=5

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One posted settlement debit.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM settlements LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,amount_cents,SUM(amount_cents) OVER(ORDER BY posted_at,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS total_cents FROM settlements WHERE id<=5

hints: Order postings by posted_at then id to break equal timestamps.
Join the original authorization to obtain account_id, then partition the running total by account.

quiz.q: What does a running SUM with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW include?
options: This row and every earlier row in the sort order
quiz.why: UNBOUNDED PRECEDING through CURRENT ROW accumulates every row so far. It counts rows in the frame, not a fixed number of days.

challenges.prompt: Return id, amount_cents and running_debits_cents for every settlement. Accumulate amount_cents by posted_at then id using a ROWS frame.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,amount_cents,SUM(amount_cents) OVER(ORDER BY posted_at,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_debits_cents FROM settlements

challenges.prompt: Return settlement_id, account_id and running_debits_cents for every settlement. Accumulate only that account’s settlements, ordered by posted_at then settlement id.
challenges.answer: SELECT s.id AS settlement_id,a.account_id,SUM(s.amount_cents) OVER(PARTITION BY a.account_id ORDER BY s.posted_at,s.id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_debits_cents FROM settlements s JOIN authorizations a ON a.id=s.authorization_id

lessons.title: Logical query processing & row grain
lessons.reason: Grouped totals contrast with a window retaining every input row; the quiz tests logical WHERE order.
lessons.concept: Think FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. This is a logical model, not a promise about physical execution. Row expressions preserve rows, aggregates collapse them, and windows add context without collapsing.

walkthrough.title: Start with rows
walkthrough.description: One row is one paid order line.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,customer_id,quantity FROM store_orders WHERE status='paid';

walkthrough.title: Aggregate
walkthrough.description: Customers become the output grain.
walkthrough.query: SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM store_orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY customer_id;

walkthrough.title: Filter groups
walkthrough.description: HAVING works on the totals, then ordering shapes the output.
walkthrough.query: SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM store_orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(quantity)>2 ORDER BY units DESC,customer_id

walkthrough.title: Keep individual rows instead
walkthrough.description: A window attaches the customer total while retaining order rows.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,customer_id,quantity,SUM(quantity) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_units FROM store_orders WHERE status='paid'

hints: WHERE excludes unpaid rows before either calculation.
GROUP BY reduces rows; SUM OVER(PARTITION BY ...) preserves each paid order.

quiz.q: When are row conditions in WHERE applied relative to GROUP BY?
quiz.why: The logical flow filters source rows with WHERE before grouping them. HAVING then filters the groups.

challenges.prompt: Return customer_id and units for paid store_orders grouped by customer; keep groups with units >2. Sort units descending, then customer_id ascending.
challenges.answer: SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM store_orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(quantity)>2 ORDER BY units DESC,customer_id

challenges.prompt: Keep every paid order row and return id, customer_id, quantity and customer_units (sum of paid quantity for that customer using a window).
challenges.answer: SELECT id,customer_id,quantity,SUM(quantity) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_units FROM store_orders WHERE status='paid'

lessons.title: Compare rows with LAG
lessons.reason: Flight predecessor selection transfers from all scheduled rows to operated rows before LAG; cancellations change membership.
lessons.concept: LAG reads a value from the previous row in an explicitly ordered partition. Filtering before the window changes what previous means. A cancelled flight has no departure delay; preserving that NULL differs from skipping the cancelled row.
lessons.example: SELECT id,route_id,LAG(departure_delay_minutes) OVER(PARTITION BY route_id ORDER BY scheduled_departure,id) AS previous_delay FROM flights;

walkthrough.title: Inspect a route timeline
walkthrough.description: Scheduled flights include cancellations with unknown delays.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,route_id,scheduled_departure,cancelled,departure_delay_minutes FROM flights WHERE route_id=32 ORDER BY scheduled_departure,id

walkthrough.title: Compare the previous scheduled leg
walkthrough.description: LAG follows the window order and retains NULL from a cancelled predecessor.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,route_id,LAG(departure_delay_minutes) OVER(PARTITION BY route_id ORDER BY scheduled_departure,id) AS previous_delay FROM flights WHERE route_id=32

hints: Partition by route_id and order by scheduled_departure,id.
For the second task, filter cancelled=0 before applying LAG, then subtract the previous delay.

quiz.q: What does LAG(value) return for the first row in a partition when no default is supplied?
options: The last value in the partition
quiz.why: There is no previous row at the start of a partition, so LAG returns NULL unless you supply a default.

challenges.prompt: Return id, route_id and previous_delay for every scheduled flight. previous_delay is the departure_delay_minutes of the previous scheduled flight on that route, ordered by scheduled_departure then id. Keep cancelled flights and their NULL delays.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,route_id,LAG(departure_delay_minutes) OVER(PARTITION BY route_id ORDER BY scheduled_departure,id) AS previous_delay FROM flights

challenges.prompt: Return id, route_id and delay_change for operated flights only (cancelled=0). Compare departure_delay_minutes with the previous operated flight on the same route, ordered by scheduled_departure then id. The first operated flight on each route has NULL change.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,route_id,departure_delay_minutes-LAG(departure_delay_minutes) OVER(PARTITION BY route_id ORDER BY scheduled_departure,id) AS delay_change FROM flights WHERE cancelled=0

lessons.title: Latest row per group
lessons.reason: Latest-per-customer transfers to highest-per-category with a different tie rule.
lessons.concept: Use a CTE with ROW_NUMBER sorted newest-first, then filter to row number 1. A window result cannot be filtered by WHERE in the same query block.

walkthrough.title: See multiple rows per customer
walkthrough.description: Customers can have several store_orders. Choosing the latest one needs an order and a way to keep only rank 1.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, customer_id, ordered_at FROM store_orders ORDER BY customer_id, ordered_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 12;

walkthrough.title: Keep the newest row per group
walkthrough.description: ROW_NUMBER ordered by newest first marks the latest order as 1. Filtering rn = 1 keeps one row per customer.

hints: Number rows inside a CTE, then filter outside it.
Keep rn = 1 in the outer WHERE.

quiz.q: How do you keep one latest row per customer with ROW_NUMBER?
options: Number all rows globally and keep the first
Partition by customer, order newest first with a tie-breaker, then filter rn = 1 in an outer query
quiz.why: Partitioning separates store_customers. Ordering identifies the latest row; an outer query filters the window result.

challenges.prompt: Return id, customer_id and ordered_at for the latest order per customer; break date ties by highest id.
challenges.answer: WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at DESC,id DESC) AS rn FROM store_orders) SELECT id,customer_id,ordered_at FROM ranked WHERE rn=1

challenges.prompt: Return name, category and price for the most expensive product per category; break price ties by lowest id.
challenges.answer: WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS rn FROM store_products) SELECT name,category,price FROM ranked WHERE rn=1

lessons.title: LEAD & the next event
lessons.reason: Logistics LEAD uses physical time and an id tie-breaker; transfer calculates seconds and retains final NULLs and raw retries.
lessons.concept: LEAD reads a value from the next row in an ordered partition. Order physical scans by occurred_at and id, not by when they arrived in the system. The final row in a package partition has no successor and returns NULL.
lessons.example: SELECT id,occurred_at,LEAD(occurred_at) OVER(ORDER BY occurred_at,id) AS next_at FROM tracking_events WHERE package_id=1

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One received tracking scan, including repeated deliveries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM tracking_events LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,occurred_at,LEAD(occurred_at) OVER(ORDER BY occurred_at,id) AS next_at FROM tracking_events WHERE package_id=1

hints: Partition by package_id; order by occurred_at then id.
Subtract unixepoch(occurred_at) from unixepoch of the next physical timestamp.

quiz.q: What does LEAD(value) return when there is no next row and no default is supplied?
quiz.why: LEAD reads the next row in the ordered partition. At the end, it returns NULL unless a default is supplied.

challenges.prompt: Return id, package_id and next_scan_at for every tracking_events row. The next scan is within the package, ordered by occurred_at then id.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,package_id,LEAD(occurred_at) OVER(PARTITION BY package_id ORDER BY occurred_at,id) AS next_scan_at FROM tracking_events

challenges.prompt: Return id and seconds_to_next for every received scan. Use the same package order and subtract current occurred_at from the next occurred_at in seconds. The last scan gets NULL.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,unixepoch(LEAD(occurred_at) OVER(PARTITION BY package_id ORDER BY occurred_at,id))-unixepoch(occurred_at) AS seconds_to_next FROM tracking_events

lessons.title: FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE & frames
lessons.reason: IoT full-frame LAST_VALUE transfers to deviation from FIRST_VALUE; default frame and baseline semantics differ.
lessons.concept: FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE read values from a window frame. To repeat a device’s final observed value on every row, the frame must include UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. For a change from baseline, subtract the first observed value in the device partition.
lessons.example: SELECT observed_at,temperature_c,LAST_VALUE(temperature_c) OVER(ORDER BY observed_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS final_value FROM sensor_readings WHERE device_id=1

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One device and observation timestamp.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM sensor_readings LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT observed_at,temperature_c,LAST_VALUE(temperature_c) OVER(ORDER BY observed_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS final_value FROM sensor_readings WHERE device_id=1

hints: Partition by device_id and order by observed_at.
For the final value use the entire partition frame. For a baseline change use FIRST_VALUE and round only the result.

quiz.q: Why does LAST_VALUE often return the current row?
options: The default ordered frame may end at the current row
It only works with one row
quiz.why: Extend the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING to include the final row in the partition.

challenges.prompt: Return device_id, observed_at and final_temperature_c for every sensor_readings row. Repeat that device’s final observed temperature across all its rows.
challenges.answer: SELECT device_id,observed_at,LAST_VALUE(temperature_c) OVER(PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY observed_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS final_temperature_c FROM sensor_readings
