challenges.prompt: Return device_id, observed_at and change_from_first_c: temperature_c minus the device’s first observed temperature, rounded to two decimals.
challenges.answer: SELECT device_id,observed_at,ROUND(temperature_c-FIRST_VALUE(temperature_c) OVER(PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY observed_at),2) AS change_from_first_c FROM sensor_readings

lessons.title: Rolling averages & missing dates
lessons.reason: Weather observed-row averaging transfers to a complete calendar; absent temperatures stay unknown rather than invented zeros.
lessons.concept: A ROWS window counts observations, not elapsed calendar days. To represent every calendar date, build the date grid first and left join observations. Missing temperature is unknown, not zero; AVG ignores missing values within the calendar frame.
lessons.example: SELECT date,raw_value/10.0 AS tmax_c,AVG(raw_value/10.0) OVER(ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS mean_c FROM daily_weather WHERE station_id='USW00094728' AND element='TMAX' AND quality_flag IS NULL AND raw_value IS NOT NULL

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One station-date maximum-temperature measurement or expected calendar slot.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM daily_weather LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT date,raw_value/10.0 AS tmax_c,AVG(raw_value/10.0) OVER(ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS mean_c FROM daily_weather WHERE station_id='USW00094728' AND element='TMAX' AND quality_flag IS NULL AND raw_value IS NOT NULL

hints: For the observed-row task, filter usable TMAX observations before the window.
For calendar days, CROSS JOIN stations and calendar, LEFT JOIN usable TMAX, then apply the same three-row frame within each station.

quiz.q: A calendar date has no usable temperature. What should a calendar rolling average do?
options: Keep its calendar slot and ignore its NULL value in AVG
Remove the date before defining the frame
quiz.why: Keeping the date preserves the time window. NULL represents unknown temperature; zero would invent a measurement.

challenges.prompt: Return station_id, date and rolling_tmax_c for usable TMAX observations only. Average current and previous two observed temperatures, divide raw tenths by 10.0 and round to two decimals. Usable means raw_value non-NULL and quality_flag NULL. Order by station_id,date.
challenges.answer: SELECT station_id,date,ROUND(AVG(raw_value/10.0) OVER(PARTITION BY station_id ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW),2) AS rolling_tmax_c FROM daily_weather WHERE element='TMAX' AND raw_value IS NOT NULL AND quality_flag IS NULL ORDER BY station_id,date

challenges.prompt: Return station_id, date and rolling_tmax_c for every station and calendar date. Average usable TMAX values in the current and previous two calendar dates, ignoring missing values; an entirely missing window is NULL. Round Celsius averages to two decimals. Order by station_id,date.
challenges.answer: SELECT s.id AS station_id,c.date,ROUND(AVG(w.raw_value/10.0) OVER(PARTITION BY s.id ORDER BY c.date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW),2) AS rolling_tmax_c FROM stations s CROSS JOIN calendar c LEFT JOIN daily_weather w ON w.station_id=s.id AND w.date=c.date AND w.element='TMAX' AND w.quality_flag IS NULL ORDER BY s.id,c.date

lessons.title: Share of total with windows
lessons.reason: Energy global fuel share transfers to regional denominators; ratio of sums and zero-denominator handling are explicit.
lessons.concept: A window total can turn grouped measures into shares without collapsing the grouped rows. Choose the denominator deliberately: generation across the whole grid differs from generation within each region.
lessons.example: SELECT fuel,output_mw,ROUND(100.0*output_mw/NULLIF(SUM(output_mw) OVER(),0),2) AS share_pct FROM generation WHERE region_id=1 AND hour='2025-01-01T00:00:00Z'

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One fuel summary, then one region-fuel summary.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM generation LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT fuel,output_mw,ROUND(100.0*output_mw/NULLIF(SUM(output_mw) OVER(),0),2) AS share_pct FROM generation WHERE region_id=1 AND hour='2025-01-01T00:00:00Z'

hints: Aggregate output_mw by fuel before computing the window denominator.
Partition the denominator by region_id when comparing fuel mix within regions.

quiz.q: Why use SUM(value) OVER () as the denominator for share of total?
options: It repeats the overall total while keeping each detail row
It collapses all rows into one
It selects only the largest value
quiz.why: The window aggregate exposes the total on each row. Divide each row’s value by that total, using appropriate numeric and zero-denominator handling.

challenges.prompt: Return fuel, output_mw and share_pct of all generation. Sum output_mw by fuel; share_pct is 0–100, rounded to two decimals, or NULL if the denominator is zero.
challenges.answer: SELECT fuel,SUM(output_mw) AS output_mw,ROUND(100.0*SUM(output_mw)/NULLIF(SUM(SUM(output_mw)) OVER(),0),2) AS share_pct FROM generation GROUP BY fuel

challenges.prompt: Return region_id, fuel, output_mw and share_pct of that region’s generation, rounded to two decimals. Use NULL if a region’s total is zero.
challenges.answer: SELECT region_id,fuel,SUM(output_mw) AS output_mw,ROUND(100.0*SUM(output_mw)/NULLIF(SUM(SUM(output_mw)) OVER(PARTITION BY region_id),0),2) AS share_pct FROM generation GROUP BY region_id,fuel

lessons.title: Top N per group & ties
lessons.reason: Exactly two items transfers to all top ties; ROW_NUMBER and DENSE_RANK answer different business contracts.
lessons.concept: Aggregate watched seconds per video, then rank videos within creator. ROW_NUMBER gives an exact N with a tie-breaker; DENSE_RANK includes ties and may return more than N. Make the tie policy explicit.
lessons.example:
WITH totals AS(SELECT v.creator_id,v.id AS video_id,
SUM(w.watch_seconds) AS watch_seconds FROM videos v
JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id=v.id GROUP BY v.id,v.creator_id),
ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY creator_id
ORDER BY watch_seconds DESC,video_id) AS rn FROM totals)
SELECT creator_id,video_id,watch_seconds FROM ranked WHERE rn<=2;

walkthrough.title: Rank videos inside each creator
walkthrough.description: Top-N per group needs a partition. Aggregate watch time per video, then number videos within each creator.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT v.creator_id, v.id AS video_id, SUM(w.watch_seconds) AS watch_seconds
FROM videos v JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id = v.id
GROUP BY v.creator_id, v.id
ORDER BY v.creator_id, watch_seconds DESC;

walkthrough.title: Keep the top rows per group
walkthrough.description: ROW_NUMBER or RANK inside the creator partition selects the top videos. Ties need an explicit rule.
walkthrough.query:
WITH totals AS(SELECT v.creator_id,v.id AS video_id,
SUM(w.watch_seconds) AS watch_seconds FROM videos v
JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id=v.id GROUP BY v.id,v.creator_id),
ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY creator_id
ORDER BY watch_seconds DESC,video_id) AS rn FROM totals)
SELECT creator_id,video_id,watch_seconds FROM ranked WHERE rn<=2;

hints: Aggregate per video before ranking within creator.
Use a video_id tie-breaker only when you need an exact number of rows.

quiz.q: To return exactly two rows per group with deterministic tie handling, which function fits?
quiz.why: ROW_NUMBER assigns unique positions. A stable tie-breaker determines which tied rows occupy the two positions; rank functions can include more rows when ties are kept.

challenges.prompt: Return creator_id, video_id and watch_seconds for the top 2 watched videos per creator, excluding videos with no events. Rank by total seconds descending, break ties by smallest video_id.
challenges.answer: WITH totals AS(SELECT v.creator_id,v.id AS video_id,SUM(w.watch_seconds) AS watch_seconds FROM videos v JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id=v.id GROUP BY v.id,v.creator_id),ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY creator_id ORDER BY watch_seconds DESC,video_id) AS rn FROM totals) SELECT creator_id,video_id,watch_seconds FROM ranked WHERE rn<=2

challenges.prompt: Return creator_id, video_id and watch_seconds for each creator's most-watched video(s), including ties. Exclude videos with no events.
challenges.answer: WITH totals AS(SELECT v.creator_id,v.id AS video_id,SUM(w.watch_seconds) AS watch_seconds FROM videos v JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id=v.id GROUP BY v.id,v.creator_id),ranked AS(SELECT *,DENSE_RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY creator_id ORDER BY watch_seconds DESC) AS rn FROM totals) SELECT creator_id,video_id,watch_seconds FROM ranked WHERE rn=1

lessons.title: NTILE & balanced ranking buckets
lessons.reason: Sports appearance buckets transfer from league-wide to team partitions; NTILE can split equal minutes.
lessons.concept: NTILE distributes ordered rows into buckets with similar row counts. It does not preserve equal values in the same bucket. Define a deterministic tie-breaker and choose whether buckets should restart by team.
lessons.example: SELECT game_id,player_id,minutes,NTILE(3) OVER(ORDER BY minutes DESC,player_id) AS bucket FROM appearances WHERE game_id=1

walkthrough.title: Inspect the input grain
walkthrough.description: One player appearance, identified by game_id and player_id.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM appearances LIMIT 5

walkthrough.title: Run a focused example
walkthrough.description: This example uses a limited group or a different summary grain. Apply the concept to the full task and check its boundaries.
walkthrough.query: SELECT game_id,player_id,minutes,NTILE(3) OVER(ORDER BY minutes DESC,player_id) AS bucket FROM appearances WHERE game_id=1

hints: Use minutes descending, then game_id and player_id for deterministic ties.
Join players to get registered team_id and partition the buckets by team.

quiz.q: What does NTILE(3) do to six ordered rows?
options: Assigns them to three buckets of two rows each
Returns only the first three rows
quiz.why: NTILE divides the ordered rows into roughly equal buckets while keeping the rows visible. When six rows divide evenly into three buckets, each gets two.

challenges.prompt: Return game_id, player_id, minutes and bucket using NTILE(4) across appearances, ordered in the window by minutes descending, game_id then player_id.
challenges.answer: SELECT game_id,player_id,minutes,NTILE(4) OVER(ORDER BY minutes DESC,game_id,player_id) AS bucket FROM appearances

challenges.prompt: Return game_id, player_id, team_id and bucket using NTILE(2) within each player’s registered team. Order by minutes descending, game_id then player_id.
challenges.answer: SELECT a.game_id,a.player_id,p.team_id,NTILE(2) OVER(PARTITION BY p.team_id ORDER BY a.minutes DESC,a.game_id,a.player_id) AS bucket FROM appearances a JOIN players p ON p.id=a.player_id

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs
lessons.reason: Recursive numeric anchor transfers to a multi-level developer hierarchy; acyclic input is a declared assumption.
lessons.concept: A recursive CTE has an anchor row and a recursive step joined by UNION ALL. The step uses the previous result until its stopping condition is false. Always include a termination condition.

walkthrough.title: Start from a base row
walkthrough.description: A recursive CTE needs an anchor member. Here the sequence begins at 1 before the recursive step adds 1.
walkthrough.query: SELECT 1 AS n;

walkthrough.title: Grow the sequence recursively
walkthrough.description: UNION ALL attaches rows produced from previous rows until the WHERE stop condition fails.

hints: For a number sequence, anchor with SELECT 1 and stop at the upper bound.
For a hierarchy, anchor at manager_id IS NULL and join children on child.manager_id = parent.id. Carry depth + 1.

quiz.q: Which part of a recursive CTE supplies the starting rows?
quiz.why: The anchor supplies the starting rows. The recursive part derives subsequent rows from the current result.

challenges.prompt: Use a recursive CTE to return n with integers 1 through 5.
challenges.answer: WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS(SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM numbers WHERE n<5) SELECT n FROM numbers

challenges.prompt: Return developer_id and depth for every developer reachable from a root whose manager_id is NULL. Roots have depth 0; each reporting edge adds 1. The supplied management graph is acyclic. Use a recursive CTE to follow all levels.
challenges.answer: WITH RECURSIVE tree(developer_id,depth) AS (SELECT id,0 FROM developers WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT d.id,t.depth+1 FROM developers d JOIN tree t ON d.manager_id=t.developer_id) SELECT developer_id,depth FROM tree

lessons.title: Query plans & indexes
lessons.reason: Keeps SQLite plan inspection conceptual; these two tasks stay lesson-only because they require Explain mode.
lessons.concept: An index can help SQLite find or order rows efficiently. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows SCAN versus SEARCH and index use. Indexes cost storage and slow writes; the optimizer may still scan a tiny table.
lessons.example:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT name FROM store_customers WHERE city='Chicago';

walkthrough.title: Run the filtered lookup
walkthrough.description: This is the query whose plan you will inspect. Note the city predicate—indexes may later speed this path.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name FROM store_customers WHERE city = 'Chicago';

walkthrough.title: Read the query plan
walkthrough.description: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN names the access strategy (scan, search, and so on). Indexes change which path the engine picks.
walkthrough.query: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT name FROM store_customers WHERE city = 'Chicago';

hints: Write the SELECT normally; choose Explain for its plan.
Plan output is informative; submit the normal query to check the answer.

quiz.q: What does EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN show?
options: The exact number of milliseconds every future run will take
quiz.why: A plan shows how SQLite intends to access data. It does not measure execution time or prove a production speedup.

challenges.prompt: Show name for Chicago store_customers. Run the reference with Explain mode to inspect the plan.
challenges.answer: SELECT name FROM store_customers WHERE city='Chicago'

challenges.prompt: Show id and quantity for paid store_orders. Inspect its plan with Explain mode.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,quantity FROM store_orders WHERE status='paid'

lessons.title: Capstone: customer insights
lessons.reason: Capstone combines joins, aggregates and dense ranking at two reporting grains; repetition is deliberate synthesis.
lessons.concept: Combine filtering, joins, aggregation and ranking to answer a business question. First compute each customer's paid revenue, then rank those customer totals. Write one stage at a time.

walkthrough.title: Assemble paid revenue pieces
walkthrough.description: Customer insights join store_customers, paid store_orders, and product prices before summing. Check the join keys first.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT c.name, o.quantity, p.price, o.status
FROM store_customers c
JOIN store_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN store_products p ON p.id = o.product_id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
LIMIT 8;

walkthrough.title: Summarize paid revenue per customer
walkthrough.description: The capstone CTE pattern computes paid_revenue, then the outer query ranks or filters those totals.
walkthrough.query:
WITH revenue AS (
  SELECT c.name, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS paid_revenue
  FROM store_customers c
  JOIN store_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
  JOIN store_products p ON p.id = o.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY c.name
) SELECT name, paid_revenue FROM revenue ORDER BY paid_revenue DESC;

hints: Compute paid revenue in a grouped CTE.
Rank the revenue column in the outer query.

quiz.q: Why calculate customer revenue before ranking store_customers?
options: To rank one total per customer instead of individual order lines
To remove all store_customers with tied totals
quiz.why: The reporting grain is one customer. Aggregate order-line revenue to that grain before ranking.

challenges.prompt: Show name, paid_revenue and revenue_rank for store_customers with paid store_orders. Use DENSE_RANK, highest revenue first in the rank calculation.
challenges.answer: WITH revenue AS(SELECT c.name,SUM(o.quantity*p.price) AS paid_revenue FROM store_customers c JOIN store_orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id JOIN store_products p ON p.id=o.product_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id,c.name) SELECT name,paid_revenue,DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY paid_revenue DESC) AS revenue_rank FROM revenue

challenges.prompt: Show category, paid_revenue and revenue_rank for product categories with paid store_orders. Use DENSE_RANK by revenue descending.
challenges.answer: WITH revenue AS(SELECT p.category,SUM(o.quantity*p.price) AS paid_revenue FROM store_orders o JOIN store_products p ON p.id=o.product_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY p.category) SELECT category,paid_revenue,DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY paid_revenue DESC) AS revenue_rank FROM revenue

lessons.title: Deduplicate event retries
lessons.reason: Latest ingestion per event key transfers to summaries after deduplication; id resolves ingestion-time ties.
lessons.concept: Ingestion retries can produce several physical rows for one logical event. Define the event key and which version wins. ROW_NUMBER per event_key, ordered by ingested_at and id descending, keeps the latest version.

walkthrough.title: Find event retries
walkthrough.description: Logical event a has more than one physical row.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM social_events WHERE event_key='a' ORDER BY ingested_at,id;

walkthrough.title: Number versions
walkthrough.description: The latest ingestion wins; id breaks timestamp ties.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,event_key,ingested_at,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_key ORDER BY ingested_at DESC,id DESC) AS rn FROM social_events ORDER BY event_key,rn;

walkthrough.title: Keep one version
walkthrough.description: DISTINCT on all columns cannot remove retries whose id or ingested_at changed.
walkthrough.query: WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_key ORDER BY ingested_at DESC,id DESC) AS rn FROM social_events) SELECT id,event_key,member_id FROM ranked WHERE rn=1

hints: The partition is the logical event_key, not member_id.
Filter rn=1 before counting events.

quiz.q: Why deduplicate retries by a stable event identifier before counting events?
options: Retries can otherwise count the same logical event more than once
Every repeated value is necessarily a retry
Deduplication makes every event happen on the same date
quiz.why: Multiple source versions can represent one logical event. A declared identifier and deterministic version order choose one record.

challenges.prompt: Return id, event_key and member_id for the latest ingested row of each event_key. Break ingestion ties by highest id.
challenges.answer: WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_key ORDER BY ingested_at DESC,id DESC) AS rn FROM social_events) SELECT id,event_key,member_id FROM ranked WHERE rn=1

challenges.prompt: After keeping the latest ingested row per event_key (tie: highest id), return event_type and event_count by event_type.
challenges.answer: WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_key ORDER BY ingested_at DESC,id DESC) AS rn FROM social_events) SELECT event_type,COUNT(*) AS event_count FROM ranked WHERE rn=1 GROUP BY event_type

lessons.title: Daily active users & engagement
lessons.reason: Distinct daily audience transfers to minutes per active viewer; numerator and denominator share the same day population.
lessons.concept: DAU counts distinct people with activity on a calendar day, not event rows. Define engagement separately: here it is total seconds divided by active viewers. This result includes observed dates only.
lessons.example:
SELECT date(watched_at) AS day,COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id)
AS active_viewers FROM watch_events GROUP BY day;

walkthrough.title: Bucket watches by calendar day
walkthrough.description: Daily active users need a day grain. date(watched_at) turns timestamps into calendar days before counting viewers.
walkthrough.query: SELECT date(watched_at) AS day, viewer_id FROM watch_events ORDER BY day, viewer_id LIMIT 12;

walkthrough.title: Count distinct viewers per day
walkthrough.description: COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id) counts people, not events. Grouping by day produces the DAU series.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT date(watched_at) AS day, COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id) AS active_viewers
FROM watch_events GROUP BY date(watched_at);

hints: A viewer can have several watch events on the same day.
Use COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id) and convert seconds to minutes with 60.0.

quiz.q: One viewer watches three videos on the same day. How much do they contribute to daily active viewers?
options: Zero unless all videos are different
quiz.why: Daily active viewers counts DISTINCT viewer_id for the day. Watch events and engagement seconds are separate measures.

challenges.prompt: Return day (YYYY-MM-DD) and active_viewers (distinct viewers) for every observed watch date.
challenges.answer: SELECT date(watched_at) AS day,COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id) AS active_viewers FROM watch_events GROUP BY day

challenges.prompt: Return day, active_viewers and minutes_per_active_viewer, rounded to 2 decimals, for each observed watch date.
challenges.answer: SELECT date(watched_at) AS day,COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id) AS active_viewers,ROUND(SUM(watch_seconds)/60.0/COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id),2) AS minutes_per_active_viewer FROM watch_events GROUP BY day

lessons.title: Ordered conversion funnels
lessons.reason: Ordered funnel counts transfer to member-level evidence; earliest valid next steps prevent unordered event membership shortcuts.
lessons.concept: A funnel is an ordered journey. Find the first view, then the first signup on or after that view, then the first purchase on or after signup. A purchase that happens before signup does not complete this funnel. Equal timestamps are allowed here.
lessons.example:
-- Build one row per member at each stage.
WITH views AS(SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id), signups AS(SELECT v.member_id,v.viewed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS signed_at FROM views v LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=v.member_id AND e.event_type='signup' AND e.event_at>=v.viewed_at GROUP BY v.member_id,v.viewed_at), funnel AS(SELECT s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS purchased_at FROM signups s LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=s.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=s.signed_at GROUP BY s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS viewed,COUNT(signed_at) AS signed_up,
COUNT(purchased_at) AS purchased FROM funnel;

walkthrough.title: Find first views
walkthrough.description: The denominator is members who entered the funnel.
walkthrough.query: SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id;

walkthrough.title: Reconstruct valid stages
walkthrough.description: Observe member 3: the purchase before view is ignored, and a later valid purchase is kept.
walkthrough.query: WITH views AS(SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id), signups AS(SELECT v.member_id,v.viewed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS signed_at FROM views v LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=v.member_id AND e.event_type='signup' AND e.event_at>=v.viewed_at GROUP BY v.member_id,v.viewed_at), funnel AS(SELECT s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS purchased_at FROM signups s LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=s.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=s.signed_at GROUP BY s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at) SELECT * FROM funnel;

walkthrough.title: Count people at each stage
walkthrough.description: LEFT JOIN leaves NULL at stages where a person drops off.
walkthrough.query: WITH views AS(SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id), signups AS(SELECT v.member_id,v.viewed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS signed_at FROM views v LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=v.member_id AND e.event_type='signup' AND e.event_at>=v.viewed_at GROUP BY v.member_id,v.viewed_at), funnel AS(SELECT s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS purchased_at FROM signups s LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=s.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=s.signed_at GROUP BY s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at) SELECT COUNT(*) AS viewed,COUNT(signed_at) AS signed_up,COUNT(purchased_at) AS purchased FROM funnel

hints: Make the next step conditional on the previous step’s timestamp.
Use LEFT JOIN for stage counts so drop-offs remain in the denominator.

quiz.q: A person purchases before signing up, then never purchases again. Did they finish the ordered signup → purchase funnel?
options: No, the purchase must occur on or after signup
quiz.why: Sequence is part of the metric definition. Independent event counts cannot establish an ordered journey.

challenges.prompt: Return one row: viewed, signed_up, purchased as member counts for the ordered view → signup → purchase funnel. Equal times are allowed; use each member's earliest valid next step.
challenges.answer: WITH views AS(SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id), signups AS(SELECT v.member_id,v.viewed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS signed_at FROM views v LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=v.member_id AND e.event_type='signup' AND e.event_at>=v.viewed_at GROUP BY v.member_id,v.viewed_at), funnel AS(SELECT s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS purchased_at FROM signups s LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=s.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=s.signed_at GROUP BY s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at) SELECT COUNT(*) AS viewed,COUNT(signed_at) AS signed_up,COUNT(purchased_at) AS purchased FROM funnel

challenges.prompt: Return member_id, viewed_at, signed_at and purchased_at for members who complete that ordered funnel.
challenges.answer: WITH views AS(SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id), signups AS(SELECT v.member_id,v.viewed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS signed_at FROM views v LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=v.member_id AND e.event_type='signup' AND e.event_at>=v.viewed_at GROUP BY v.member_id,v.viewed_at), funnel AS(SELECT s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS purchased_at FROM signups s LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=s.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=s.signed_at GROUP BY s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at) SELECT member_id,viewed_at,signed_at,purchased_at FROM funnel WHERE purchased_at IS NOT NULL

lessons.title: Cohorts & exact-day retention
lessons.reason: D1 and D7 are intentional repetition because cohort maturity changes at the fixed observation cutoff; second stays lesson-only.
lessons.concept: A cohort groups people by signup date. Exact-day D1 retention asks whether they return on signup +1 day, not anytime later. Count people, include non-returners, and exclude cohorts that have not matured by the observation cutoff.
lessons.example:
-- D1 retention; observation cutoff is 2025-01-15
SELECT v.signup_at AS cohort_day,COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+1 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retained_viewers,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+1 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*),2) AS retention_pct FROM viewers v WHERE v.signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-1 days') GROUP BY v.signup_at

walkthrough.title: Define mature cohorts
walkthrough.description: Each row is one viewer in a cohort that can have a D7 observation.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,signup_at,date(signup_at,'+7 days') AS return_day FROM viewers WHERE signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-7 days');

walkthrough.title: Mark exact-day returns
walkthrough.description: EXISTS counts each person at most once, even if several events occur on the return date.
walkthrough.query: SELECT v.id,v.signup_at,CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+7 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS retained FROM viewers v WHERE v.signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-7 days');

walkthrough.title: Report D7 retention
walkthrough.description: Retained people divided by all mature cohort members.
walkthrough.query: SELECT v.signup_at AS cohort_day,COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+7 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retained_viewers,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+7 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*),2) AS retention_pct FROM viewers v WHERE v.signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-7 days') GROUP BY v.signup_at

hints: The denominator is all viewers in the mature signup cohort.
Use EXISTS on the exact return date to avoid duplicating viewers.

quiz.q: Exact-day D7 retention means a user returns when?
options: Any time during the first seven days
On signup date plus seven calendar days
quiz.why: Exact-day, rolling-window, and unbounded retention use different definitions.

challenges.prompt: With observation cutoff Jan 15 2025, return cohort_day, cohort_size, retained_viewers and retention_pct (0–100, 2 decimals) for exact-day D1 retention. Include only mature cohorts.
challenges.answer: SELECT v.signup_at AS cohort_day,COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+1 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retained_viewers,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+1 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*),2) AS retention_pct FROM viewers v WHERE v.signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-1 days') GROUP BY v.signup_at

challenges.prompt: Use the same output and cutoff for exact-day D7 retention (signup date +7 days); include only mature cohorts.
challenges.answer: SELECT v.signup_at AS cohort_day,COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+7 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retained_viewers,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+7 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*),2) AS retention_pct FROM viewers v WHERE v.signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-7 days') GROUP BY v.signup_at

lessons.title: Sessionize an event stream
lessons.reason: Session counts transfer to row-level labels; first row and exact 30-minute boundaries are stated, second stays lesson-only.
lessons.concept: A session starts on a member’s first event or after a gap of at least 30 minutes. LAG finds the prior timestamp, CASE flags boundaries, and a running SUM numbers sessions. Here we use physical rows, including retries. Identical timestamps do not start a new session.

walkthrough.title: Find the previous timestamp
walkthrough.description: Order within member. Raw retries remain in this exercise.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,member_id,event_at,LAG(event_at) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id) AS previous_at FROM social_events ORDER BY member_id,event_at,id;

walkthrough.title: Number the sessions
walkthrough.description: A new boundary occurs on the first event or a gap >=1800 seconds.
walkthrough.query: WITH previous AS(SELECT *,LAG(event_at) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id) AS previous_at FROM social_events), marked AS(SELECT *,CASE WHEN previous_at IS NULL OR unixepoch(event_at)-unixepoch(previous_at)>=1800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session FROM previous), numbered AS(SELECT *,SUM(new_session) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_number FROM marked) SELECT id,member_id,session_number FROM numbered

walkthrough.title: Summarize sessions per member
walkthrough.description: The largest session number is the total number of sessions.
walkthrough.query: WITH previous AS(SELECT *,LAG(event_at) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id) AS previous_at FROM social_events), marked AS(SELECT *,CASE WHEN previous_at IS NULL OR unixepoch(event_at)-unixepoch(previous_at)>=1800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session FROM previous), numbered AS(SELECT *,SUM(new_session) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_number FROM marked) SELECT member_id,MAX(session_number) AS session_count FROM numbered GROUP BY member_id

hints: Use unixepoch differences in seconds to avoid floating date rounding.
Mark gaps >=1800 seconds, then running SUM the markers per member.

quiz.q: With a gap rule of at least 30 minutes, does a 30-minute gap start a new session?
quiz.why: The boundary is inclusive. Integer timestamp differences keep that definition precise.

challenges.prompt: Using raw social_events, return member_id and session_count. Start a new session on the first event or a gap of at least 30 minutes; order by event_at then id per member.
challenges.answer: WITH previous AS(SELECT *,LAG(event_at) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id) AS previous_at FROM social_events), marked AS(SELECT *,CASE WHEN previous_at IS NULL OR unixepoch(event_at)-unixepoch(previous_at)>=1800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session FROM previous), numbered AS(SELECT *,SUM(new_session) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_number FROM marked) SELECT member_id,MAX(session_number) AS session_count FROM numbered GROUP BY member_id

challenges.prompt: Using the same rule, return id, member_id and session_number for every raw social event.
challenges.answer: WITH previous AS(SELECT *,LAG(event_at) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id) AS previous_at FROM social_events), marked AS(SELECT *,CASE WHEN previous_at IS NULL OR unixepoch(event_at)-unixepoch(previous_at)>=1800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session FROM previous), numbered AS(SELECT *,SUM(new_session) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_number FROM marked) SELECT id,member_id,session_number FROM numbered

lessons.title: Multi-grain joins without fan-out
lessons.reason: Request count transfers to successful tokens while independently aggregated invoices preserve account grain.
lessons.concept: Requests and invoices each have many rows per account. Joining raw tables creates requests × invoices and inflates sums. Aggregate each side to one row per account before joining; keep accounts with zero on either side.
lessons.example:
WITH usage AS(SELECT account_id,COUNT(*) AS request_count
FROM ai_requests GROUP BY account_id), billing AS(
SELECT account_id,SUM(billed_amount) AS billed_amount
FROM invoices GROUP BY account_id)
SELECT a.id,COALESCE(u.request_count,0) AS request_count,
COALESCE(b.billed_amount,0) AS billed_amount FROM ai_accounts a
LEFT JOIN usage u ON u.account_id=a.id
LEFT JOIN billing b ON b.account_id=a.id;

walkthrough.title: Observe join fan-out
walkthrough.description: Every request pairs with every invoice for the same account. Watch request 1 appear twice.
walkthrough.query: SELECT r.id AS request_id,i.id AS invoice_id,i.billed_amount FROM ai_requests r JOIN invoices i ON i.account_id=r.account_id WHERE r.account_id=1;

walkthrough.title: Summarize requests first
walkthrough.description: One row per account is a safe grain for the final join.
walkthrough.query: SELECT account_id,COUNT(*) AS request_count FROM ai_requests GROUP BY account_id;

walkthrough.title: Summarize invoices first
walkthrough.description: This is also one row per account.
walkthrough.query: SELECT account_id,SUM(billed_amount) AS billed_amount FROM invoices GROUP BY account_id;

walkthrough.title: Join summaries
walkthrough.description: Neither side can multiply the other now.
walkthrough.query: WITH usage AS(SELECT account_id,COUNT(*) AS request_count FROM ai_requests GROUP BY account_id),billing AS(SELECT account_id,SUM(billed_amount) AS billed_amount FROM invoices GROUP BY account_id) SELECT a.id,COALESCE(u.request_count,0) AS request_count,COALESCE(b.billed_amount,0) AS billed_amount FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN usage u ON u.account_id=a.id LEFT JOIN billing b ON b.account_id=a.id

hints: Choose account as the grain for both intermediate tables.
Join the summaries to accounts only after GROUP BY account_id.

quiz.q: Why aggregate requests and invoices separately before joining account totals?
options: To prevent each request from matching every invoice and multiplying totals
To discard accounts with more than one request
To force every account total to be equal
quiz.why: Both child tables can have several rows per account. Aggregating each to one row per account avoids many-to-many fan-out.

challenges.prompt: Return id, request_count and billed_amount for every account across all dates. Aggregate requests and invoices separately to avoid multiplication; use zeros for missing totals.
challenges.answer: WITH usage AS(SELECT account_id,COUNT(*) AS request_count FROM ai_requests GROUP BY account_id),billing AS(SELECT account_id,SUM(billed_amount) AS billed_amount FROM invoices GROUP BY account_id) SELECT a.id,COALESCE(u.request_count,0) AS request_count,COALESCE(b.billed_amount,0) AS billed_amount FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN usage u ON u.account_id=a.id LEFT JOIN billing b ON b.account_id=a.id

challenges.prompt: Return id, output_tokens and billed_amount for every account across all dates. Sum only successful output tokens and aggregate invoices separately. Use zeros for missing totals.
challenges.answer: WITH usage AS(SELECT account_id,SUM(output_tokens) AS output_tokens FROM ai_requests WHERE status='success' GROUP BY account_id),billing AS(SELECT account_id,SUM(billed_amount) AS billed_amount FROM invoices GROUP BY account_id) SELECT a.id,COALESCE(u.output_tokens,0) AS output_tokens,COALESCE(b.billed_amount,0) AS billed_amount FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN usage u ON u.account_id=a.id LEFT JOIN billing b ON b.account_id=a.id

lessons.title: Revenue & payment reconciliation
lessons.reason: Invoice reconciliation transfers to exceptions-only output; shared definition is retained and second stays lesson-only.
lessons.concept: Reconciliation compares independent totals. Sum invoice_payments and invoice_refunds by invoice before joining. Net collected is invoice_payments minus invoice_refunds; gap is billed minus net collected. A refund creates a gap under this definition, even when the original bill was paid.
lessons.example:
WITH paid AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS paid_amount FROM invoice_payments GROUP BY invoice_id),returned AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS refund_amount FROM invoice_refunds GROUP BY invoice_id)
SELECT i.id,i.billed_amount,
COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)-COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS net_collected,
i.billed_amount-COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)+COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS gap
FROM invoices i LEFT JOIN paid p ON p.invoice_id=i.id
LEFT JOIN returned r ON r.invoice_id=i.id;

walkthrough.title: Inspect split invoice_payments
walkthrough.description: Invoice 1 has two invoice_payments. Refunds also have multiple rows.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM invoice_payments WHERE invoice_id=1;

walkthrough.title: Aggregate invoice_payments
walkthrough.description: One summary row per invoice.
walkthrough.query: SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS paid_amount FROM invoice_payments GROUP BY invoice_id;

walkthrough.title: Aggregate invoice_refunds
walkthrough.description: Join this summary, not individual refund rows.
walkthrough.query: SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS refund_amount FROM invoice_refunds GROUP BY invoice_id;

walkthrough.title: Calculate the reconciliation gap
walkthrough.description: Unmatched invoice_payments need a separate investigation; they are not assigned to an invoice here.
walkthrough.query: WITH paid AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS paid_amount FROM invoice_payments GROUP BY invoice_id),returned AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS refund_amount FROM invoice_refunds GROUP BY invoice_id) SELECT i.id,i.billed_amount,COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)-COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS net_collected,i.billed_amount-COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)+COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS gap FROM invoices i LEFT JOIN paid p ON p.invoice_id=i.id LEFT JOIN returned r ON r.invoice_id=i.id

hints: Aggregate the two transaction tables independently.
A split payment combined with two invoice_refunds produces four joined rows unless pre-aggregated.

quiz.q: Why keep invoice totals separate from payment totals before reconciliation?
options: Invoices and invoice_payments can have different row grains
Every invoice always has exactly one payment
Joining raw rows always preserves both sums
quiz.why: An invoice can have multiple invoice_payments. Summarize each source at the reconciliation grain before comparing totals.

challenges.prompt: Return id, billed_amount, net_collected and gap for every invoice across all periods. Net collected = invoice_payments - invoice_refunds; gap = billed - net collected. Treat missing totals as zero.
challenges.answer: WITH paid AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS paid_amount FROM invoice_payments GROUP BY invoice_id),returned AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS refund_amount FROM invoice_refunds GROUP BY invoice_id) SELECT i.id,i.billed_amount,COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)-COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS net_collected,i.billed_amount-COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)+COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS gap FROM invoices i LEFT JOIN paid p ON p.invoice_id=i.id LEFT JOIN returned r ON r.invoice_id=i.id

challenges.prompt: Using the same definition, return invoice_id and gap only for invoices with nonzero gap.
challenges.answer: WITH paid AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS paid_amount FROM invoice_payments GROUP BY invoice_id),returned AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS refund_amount FROM invoice_refunds GROUP BY invoice_id), result AS(SELECT i.id AS invoice_id,i.billed_amount-COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)+COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS gap FROM invoices i LEFT JOIN paid p ON p.invoice_id=i.id LEFT JOIN returned r ON r.invoice_id=i.id) SELECT invoice_id,gap FROM result WHERE gap<>0

lessons.title: AI usage cost & contribution margin
lessons.reason: Model costs transfer to account contribution margin in a fixed month; fictional prices and non-profit limitation are explicit.
lessons.concept: Usage cost equals input tokens × input rate plus output tokens × output rate, divided by one million. These rates are fictional. Under this exercise’s rule, successful requests are chargeable; errors are excluded. Compare January billed revenue to January successful usage cost, not all-time billing.
lessons.example:
SELECT r.model,ROUND(SUM(r.input_tokens*m.input_per_million+
r.output_tokens*m.output_per_million)/1000000.0,6) AS usage_cost
FROM ai_requests r JOIN model_rates m ON m.model=r.model
WHERE r.status='success' GROUP BY r.model;

walkthrough.title: Price a request
walkthrough.description: These teaching rates are fictional, in USD per million tokens.
walkthrough.query: SELECT r.id,r.model,(r.input_tokens*m.input_per_million+r.output_tokens*m.output_per_million)/1000000.0 AS usage_cost FROM ai_requests r JOIN model_rates m ON m.model=r.model WHERE r.status='success';

walkthrough.title: Compare aligned January totals
walkthrough.description: Billed revenue and usage costs share the same account and period grain.
walkthrough.query: WITH costs AS(SELECT r.account_id,SUM(r.input_tokens*m.input_per_million+r.output_tokens*m.output_per_million)/1000000.0 AS usage_cost FROM ai_requests r JOIN model_rates m ON m.model=r.model WHERE r.status='success' AND r.requested_at>='2025-01-01' AND r.requested_at<'2025-02-01' GROUP BY r.account_id),billing AS(SELECT account_id,SUM(billed_amount) AS billed_amount FROM invoices WHERE period='2025-01' GROUP BY account_id) SELECT a.id,COALESCE(b.billed_amount,0) AS billed_amount,ROUND(COALESCE(c.usage_cost,0),6) AS usage_cost,ROUND(COALESCE(b.billed_amount,0)-COALESCE(c.usage_cost,0),6) AS contribution_margin FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN costs c ON c.account_id=a.id LEFT JOIN billing b ON b.account_id=a.id

hints: Rates are per million; divide after adding input and output charges.
Summarize both usage and billing per account before joining.

quiz.q: Is billed revenue minus model token cost the same as net profit?
options: No; other costs and invoice_refunds may still be excluded
quiz.why: This exercise defines a simplified contribution margin. It does not include all operating costs.

challenges.prompt: Return model and usage_cost in fictional USD, rounded to 6 decimals, for successful requests across all dates.
challenges.answer: SELECT r.model,ROUND(SUM(r.input_tokens*m.input_per_million+r.output_tokens*m.output_per_million)/1000000.0,6) AS usage_cost FROM ai_requests r JOIN model_rates m ON m.model=r.model WHERE r.status='success' GROUP BY r.model

challenges.prompt: Return id, billed_amount, usage_cost and contribution_margin for every account for Jan 2025. Use January invoices and successful requests only; missing totals are zero. Round cost and margin to 6 decimals. Margin = billed - usage cost.
challenges.answer: WITH costs AS(SELECT r.account_id,SUM(r.input_tokens*m.input_per_million+r.output_tokens*m.output_per_million)/1000000.0 AS usage_cost FROM ai_requests r JOIN model_rates m ON m.model=r.model WHERE r.status='success' AND r.requested_at>='2025-01-01' AND r.requested_at<'2025-02-01' GROUP BY r.account_id),billing AS(SELECT account_id,SUM(billed_amount) AS billed_amount FROM invoices WHERE period='2025-01' GROUP BY account_id) SELECT a.id,COALESCE(b.billed_amount,0) AS billed_amount,ROUND(COALESCE(c.usage_cost,0),6) AS usage_cost,ROUND(COALESCE(b.billed_amount,0)-COALESCE(c.usage_cost,0),6) AS contribution_margin FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN costs c ON c.account_id=a.id LEFT JOIN billing b ON b.account_id=a.id

lessons.title: Experiment conversion denominators
lessons.reason: Assigned-user conversion rates transfer to per-assignment flags; the same post-assignment rule preserves the denominator.
lessons.concept: Compare assigned members, including people who do nothing. A conversion is at least one purchase on or after assignment, through Jan 31. Counting purchases instead of members or using only active members biases the denominator. This query estimates rates, not statistical significance.
lessons.example:
WITH results AS(SELECT a.member_id,a.variant,CASE WHEN EXISTS(
 SELECT 1 FROM social_events e WHERE e.member_id=a.member_id
 AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=a.assigned_at
 AND e.event_at<'2025-02-01') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS converted
FROM experiment_assignments a)
SELECT variant,COUNT(*) AS assigned,SUM(converted) AS converted,
ROUND(100.0*SUM(converted)/COUNT(*),2) AS conversion_pct
FROM results GROUP BY variant;

walkthrough.title: See assignment and conversion pieces
walkthrough.description: Experiment math needs a clear denominator: assigned members per variant. Conversion checks for a later success event.
walkthrough.query: SELECT member_id, variant, assigned_at FROM experiment_assignments ORDER BY variant, member_id;

walkthrough.title: Keep the assignment denominator
walkthrough.description: Count assigned members first, then mark who converted. Filtering to converters before counting shrinks the denominator incorrectly.
walkthrough.query:
WITH results AS(SELECT a.member_id,a.variant,CASE WHEN EXISTS(
 SELECT 1 FROM social_events e WHERE e.member_id=a.member_id
 AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=a.assigned_at
 AND e.event_at<'2025-02-01') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS converted
FROM experiment_assignments a)
SELECT variant,COUNT(*) AS assigned,SUM(converted) AS converted,
ROUND(100.0*SUM(converted)/COUNT(*),2) AS conversion_pct
FROM results GROUP BY variant;

hints: Keep the assignments table as the population.
EXISTS counts a member once regardless of purchase row count.

quiz.q: What belongs in a conversion-rate denominator for an assigned-user experiment?
options: Only users who opened the app
All assigned users in the defined population
quiz.why: Include assigned users who do nothing. Restricting the denominator to active users can bias the comparison.

challenges.prompt: Return variant, assigned, converted and conversion_pct (0–100, 2 decimals). A member converts with any purchase on/after assigned_at and before Feb 1 2025. Include all assigned members.
challenges.answer: WITH results AS(SELECT a.member_id,a.variant,CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM social_events e WHERE e.member_id=a.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=a.assigned_at AND e.event_at<'2025-02-01') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS converted FROM experiment_assignments a) SELECT variant,COUNT(*) AS assigned,SUM(converted) AS converted,ROUND(100.0*SUM(converted)/COUNT(*),2) AS conversion_pct FROM results GROUP BY variant

challenges.prompt: Return member_id, variant and converted (1 or 0) for every assignment using the same post-assignment purchase definition and cutoff.
challenges.answer: SELECT a.member_id,a.variant,CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM social_events e WHERE e.member_id=a.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=a.assigned_at AND e.event_at<'2025-02-01') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS converted FROM experiment_assignments a

lessons.title: DDL: create, alter & inspect a table
lessons.reason: Two DDL shapes intentionally reinforce structural changes and schema inspection before data mutation.
lessons.concept: DDL changes structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP. DML changes rows. Use the disposable lab to try both safely. Keep all statements in one script, ending with SELECT; the next execution starts fresh.

walkthrough.title: Inspect the empty practice surface
walkthrough.description: DDL builds structure. Start from the lab items you already have, then create a separate practice table in the next step.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, name, price FROM inventory_items ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Create and alter a table
walkthrough.description: CREATE TABLE defines columns; ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN extends the contract. Inspect with a SELECT afterward.

hints: CREATE TABLE defines columns and constraints.
SQLite exposes a table-valued pragma_table_info function for this metadata.

quiz.q: Which command changes structure rather than row contents?
quiz.why: ALTER is DDL; UPDATE and DELETE modify row contents.

challenges.prompt: Create practice_people with id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and name TEXT; add city TEXT with ALTER TABLE. Return name and type from pragma_table_info('practice_people').
challenges.answer: CREATE TABLE practice_people(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,name TEXT); ALTER TABLE practice_people ADD COLUMN city TEXT; SELECT name,type FROM pragma_table_info('practice_people')

challenges.prompt: Create practice_totals with account_id INTEGER and total REAL. Return name and type from pragma_table_info('practice_totals').
challenges.answer: CREATE TABLE practice_totals(account_id INTEGER,total REAL); SELECT name,type FROM pragma_table_info('practice_totals')

lessons.title: DML: INSERT, UPDATE & DELETE
lessons.reason: Targeted insertion/update/delete transfers to predicate-based bulk changes on isolated logistics inventory.
lessons.concept: INSERT adds rows; UPDATE changes matching rows; DELETE removes matching rows. Use WHERE to constrain modifications. These exercises touch only disposable copies in memory and are reset on every run.

walkthrough.title: Read rows before mutation
walkthrough.description: DML changes data. Note the current inventory_items rows so you can see inserts, updates, and deletes afterward.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, name, price FROM inventory_items ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Insert, update, then delete
walkthrough.description: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes matching rows, DELETE removes them. Run the full script to see the net effect.

hints: Use a WHERE clause on each targeted UPDATE and DELETE.
The base table starts with ids 1,2,3 on every execution.

quiz.q: Why include a WHERE condition in a targeted UPDATE?
options: It limits which existing rows are changed
It guarantees a new row is inserted
quiz.why: UPDATE modifies matching rows. Without WHERE, every row is eligible; inspect the predicate before running a write.

challenges.prompt: Insert lab item (4, Pen, 8); add 5 to price for id=1; delete id=2. Return id, name, price for remaining items.
challenges.answer: INSERT INTO inventory_items VALUES(4,'Pen',8); UPDATE inventory_items SET price=price+5 WHERE id=1; DELETE FROM inventory_items WHERE id=2; SELECT id,name,price FROM inventory_items

challenges.prompt: Double every lab item price below 50, then delete items with price >100. Return id, name, price.
challenges.answer: UPDATE inventory_items SET price=price*2 WHERE price<50; DELETE FROM inventory_items WHERE price>100; SELECT id,name,price FROM inventory_items

lessons.title: Constraints protect the data contract
lessons.reason: Nonnegative quantity and unique email test different constraints; NULL requires its own NOT NULL contract.
lessons.concept: PRIMARY KEY identifies rows; NOT NULL requires a value; UNIQUE prevents duplicate values; CHECK enforces a condition. SQLite CHECK passes NULL unless you also use NOT NULL. Foreign-key enforcement needs PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON; the lab enables it.

walkthrough.title: See data that constraints will protect
walkthrough.description: Constraints reject invalid writes. Think about NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY, and CHECK before creating inventory.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, name, price FROM inventory_items ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Declare constraints on create
walkthrough.description: PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, and CHECK(quantity >= 0) encode the data contract at write time.

hints: Declare constraints in the CREATE statement, not only in the SELECT.
Try a second run with a negative quantity or repeated email to see the engine reject it.

quiz.q: Does CHECK(quantity>=0) alone forbid NULL in SQLite?
options: No; also use NOT NULL when missing quantity is invalid
quiz.why: CHECK passes NULL. NOT NULL is a separate constraint.

challenges.prompt: Create inventory with sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL and quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(quantity>=0); insert (A,2). Return sku and quantity.
challenges.answer: CREATE TABLE inventory(sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(quantity>=0)); INSERT INTO inventory VALUES('A',2); SELECT sku,quantity FROM inventory

challenges.prompt: Create contacts with id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE; insert (1,a@example.com) and (2,b@example.com). Return id,email.
challenges.answer: CREATE TABLE contacts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE); INSERT INTO contacts VALUES(1,'a@example.com'),(2,'b@example.com'); SELECT id,email FROM contacts

lessons.title: Transactions & savepoint recovery
lessons.reason: Whole-transaction rollback transfers to savepoint recovery with earlier pending changes preserved.
lessons.concept: A transaction groups changes. COMMIT keeps them in the current database; ROLLBACK undoes them. SAVEPOINT lets you undo a portion. In this app even committed changes vanish after the run because the entire database is disposable.

walkthrough.title: Note prices before a transaction
walkthrough.description: A transaction groups changes. ROLLBACK undoes them; COMMIT would keep them until this disposable database ends.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, price FROM inventory_items ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Roll back a grouped change
walkthrough.description: BEGIN starts a transaction. After UPDATE, ROLLBACK restores the prior prices visible in the final SELECT.

hints: ROLLBACK undoes changes since BEGIN.
ROLLBACK TO partial preserves changes made before that savepoint.

quiz.q: After ROLLBACK TO a savepoint, what happens to earlier transaction changes?
options: They remain pending in the transaction
quiz.why: A savepoint rollback undoes only later changes. COMMIT or full ROLLBACK still controls the transaction.

challenges.prompt: Begin a transaction, add 10 to every lab item price, then roll back. Return id and price; all values should be original.
challenges.answer: BEGIN; UPDATE inventory_items SET price=price+10; ROLLBACK; SELECT id,price FROM inventory_items

challenges.prompt: Begin; add 5 to price for id=1; create SAVEPOINT partial; delete id=2; roll back to partial; commit. Return id and price.
challenges.answer: BEGIN; UPDATE inventory_items SET price=price+5 WHERE id=1; SAVEPOINT partial; DELETE FROM inventory_items WHERE id=2; ROLLBACK TO partial; COMMIT; SELECT id,price FROM inventory_items

lessons.title: Views: reusable query definitions
lessons.reason: Row-filtering view transfers to grouped totals view; validators check object behavior rather than copied output.
lessons.concept: A normal view is a named query definition. It is reusable without storing a snapshot of the result. A view can simplify business logic, but it is not automatically faster or slower than the equivalent query. SQLite views are read-only unless INSTEAD OF triggers support writes.

walkthrough.title: Look at the rows a view will read
walkthrough.description: A view does not copy these rows. It saves a query, and selecting the view reads the current store_orders.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, customer_id, quantity, status FROM store_orders;

walkthrough.title: Execute a complete script
walkthrough.description: All setup and the final result run together in one disposable database.

hints: CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ... stores the definition.
Query the new view in the same script.

quiz.q: What does a normal view store?
options: A snapshot of the rows at the moment you create it
A named query that runs when you select from it
Rows that exist only for the current connection
quiz.why: A view stores a query definition. Selecting from it runs that query against the current tables. It does not save a copy of the rows.

challenges.prompt: Create view paid_orders exposing id, customer_id and quantity for paid store_orders. Return those columns by selecting the view.
challenges.answer: CREATE VIEW paid_orders AS SELECT id,customer_id,quantity FROM store_orders WHERE status='paid'; SELECT id,customer_id,quantity FROM paid_orders

challenges.prompt: Create view product_totals with category and total_price (sum of price). Return category and total_price from the view.
challenges.answer: CREATE VIEW product_totals AS SELECT category,SUM(price) AS total_price FROM store_products GROUP BY category; SELECT category,total_price FROM product_totals

lessons.title: CTEs, CTAS & temporary tables
lessons.reason: Two TEMP materializations reinforce persistence within the connection versus a statement-only CTE.
lessons.concept: A CTE names an expression for one statement. A view persists a definition. CREATE TEMP TABLE ... AS SELECT materializes an intermediate result for the connection. SQL Server uses SELECT ... INTO #temp; that syntax is not SQLite. CTAS does not carry over source constraints.

walkthrough.title: Compute units you will materialize
walkthrough.description: CTAS and TEMP tables store a query result. Build the customer_units shape in your head before writing CREATE TEMP TABLE.
walkthrough.query: SELECT customer_id, SUM(quantity) AS units FROM store_orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

walkthrough.title: Materialize with CTAS
walkthrough.description: CREATE TEMP TABLE … AS SELECT stores the result for later queries in the same session.

hints: CREATE TEMP TABLE name AS SELECT ... builds the intermediate result.
The materialized result survives statements in this script, not future app runs.

quiz.q: Which object materializes its result for the current connection?
options: A temporary table created AS SELECT
quiz.why: A temp table stores intermediate rows. A view stores a query definition; SQL Server CTEs are not materialized results.

challenges.prompt: Materialize a TEMP table customer_units with customer_id and total quantity as units. Return customer_id and units for units >3.
challenges.answer: CREATE TEMP TABLE customer_units AS SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM store_orders GROUP BY customer_id; SELECT customer_id,units FROM customer_units WHERE units>3

challenges.prompt: Materialize a TEMP table category_prices with category and average price as avg_price. Return category and avg_price for avg_price >30.
challenges.answer: CREATE TEMP TABLE category_prices AS SELECT category,AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM store_products GROUP BY category; SELECT category,avg_price FROM category_prices WHERE avg_price>30

lessons.title: Triggers & visible audit effects
lessons.reason: Single-row trigger exercise transfers to multi-row updates and audit effects; second needs the first trigger definition.
lessons.concept: A trigger runs automatically after a matching event. SQLite row triggers use OLD and NEW values. They can record an audit trail but also create hidden side effects. SQL Server triggers are statement-level and use inserted/deleted tables, so their code is different.

walkthrough.title: Read prices the trigger will watch
walkthrough.description: A trigger fires on a data change. Note current prices; an UPDATE that changes price should write an audit row.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, name, price FROM inventory_items ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Define a trigger and see its effect
walkthrough.description: AFTER UPDATE OF price inserts into an audit table when OLD.price differs from NEW.price.

hints: SQLite provides OLD.price, NEW.price and NEW.id inside the trigger.
CREATE TRIGGER contains BEGIN ... END; keep it intact in the script.

quiz.q: When does an AFTER INSERT trigger run?
options: After each matching insertion into its table
Only when you manually query the trigger
Once when the table is created
quiz.why: The trigger runs in response to the declared table event. An audit trigger can insert a corresponding audit record automatically.

challenges.prompt: Create a price_audit trigger AFTER UPDATE OF price on inventory_items, logging changed prices in inventory_audit; add 5 to id=1 price. Return item_id,old_price,new_price from inventory_audit.
challenges.answer: CREATE TRIGGER price_audit AFTER UPDATE OF price ON inventory_items WHEN OLD.price<>NEW.price BEGIN INSERT INTO inventory_audit VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.price,NEW.price); END; UPDATE inventory_items SET price=price+5 WHERE id=1; SELECT item_id,old_price,new_price FROM inventory_audit

challenges.prompt: Create the same trigger, then double prices for all items with price<50. Return item_id,old_price,new_price from inventory_audit.
challenges.answer: CREATE TRIGGER price_audit AFTER UPDATE OF price ON inventory_items WHEN OLD.price<>NEW.price BEGIN INSERT INTO inventory_audit VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.price,NEW.price); END; UPDATE inventory_items SET price=price*2 WHERE price<50; SELECT item_id,old_price,new_price FROM inventory_audit

lessons.title: Stored procedures: parameters & contracts
lessons.reason: Keeps SQL Server procedure syntax as reference only; executable SQLite tasks practice retrieval contracts and parameter transfer.
lessons.concept: A SQL Server stored procedure can expose parameters, transactions, and error handling. SQLite has no CREATE PROCEDURE. Here you practice the retrieval contract in SQLite; the separate T-SQL reference shows its SQL Server wrapper. Choose procedures or external orchestration based on the system, not a blanket preference.
lessons.example: SELECT id,customer_id,quantity FROM store_orders WHERE customer_id=1;

walkthrough.title: Call out the parameter boundary
walkthrough.description: Procedures package a contract: inputs in, result set out. Here the “parameter” is customer_id = 1 in the filter.
walkthrough.query: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM store_orders ORDER BY customer_id;

walkthrough.title: Return rows for one parameter value
walkthrough.description: Filtering to a single customer_id models a parameterized lookup. Keep the contract explicit and narrow.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, customer_id, quantity FROM store_orders WHERE customer_id = 1;

hints: Treat the parameter as a defined input value.
The SQL Server wrapper is reference-only; run the retrieval query in this app.

quiz.q: Can SQLite execute CREATE PROCEDURE from the T-SQL reference?
options: No; this lesson’s procedure wrapper is SQL Server reference only
quiz.why: The SQLite engine lacks stored procedures. Practice the retrieval contract here and the wrapper in SQL Server.

challenges.prompt: For customer_id=1, return id, customer_id and quantity from store_orders. This practices a procedure’s retrieval contract; no procedure is created in SQLite.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,customer_id,quantity FROM store_orders WHERE customer_id=1

challenges.prompt: For customer_id=2, return id, customer_id and quantity for paid store_orders only.
challenges.answer: SELECT id,customer_id,quantity FROM store_orders WHERE customer_id=2 AND status='paid'

lessons.title: Indexes: observe a real access path
lessons.reason: Two indexes reinforce observing actual access paths; no unsupported speed claim from a tiny fixture.
lessons.concept: An index offers an access structure at the cost of storage and write work. Use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to see SQLite choose SCAN, SEARCH, or a covering index. Plans describe physical access; they are not measured speed. This tiny dataset cannot establish a production performance improvement.
lessons.example:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON store_orders(customer_id);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,quantity FROM store_orders WHERE customer_id=1;

walkthrough.title: Plan a lookup before indexing
walkthrough.description: Without an index, filtering store_orders by customer_id may scan. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows the current path.
walkthrough.query: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id, quantity FROM store_orders WHERE customer_id = 1;

walkthrough.title: Add an index and re-check the plan
walkthrough.description: CREATE INDEX can change the access path. Compare the new plan to the scan you saw before.
walkthrough.query:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON store_orders(customer_id);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,quantity FROM store_orders WHERE customer_id=1;

hints: CREATE INDEX index_name ON table(column).
In lab mode Query plan runs setup statements, then explains the final SELECT.

quiz.q: An index changes SCAN to SEARCH on a tiny example. What can you conclude?
options: Production latency improved by a known percentage
The optimizer chose a different access path; measure the real workload next
quiz.why: A plan provides strategy evidence. Timing, reads, selectivity, and write overhead require workload measurement.

challenges.prompt: Create idx_orders_customer on store_orders(customer_id), then return id and quantity for customer_id=1. Run Query plan after the script to inspect the final SELECT.
challenges.answer: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON store_orders(customer_id); SELECT id,quantity FROM store_orders WHERE customer_id=1

challenges.prompt: Create idx_products_category on store_products(category), then return name and price for Tech store_products.
challenges.answer: CREATE INDEX idx_products_category ON store_products(category); SELECT name,price FROM store_products WHERE category='Tech'

lessons.title: SARGable ranges, not speed commandments
lessons.reason: Month range transfers to an inclusive named-day interval expressed with an exclusive endpoint; same access-path reasoning is intentional.
lessons.concept: A direct range on an indexed column can permit an efficient lookup. Wrapping that column in a function can prevent a normal index lookup; expression indexes are a separate option. Compare real plans and preserve the result. OR, correlated subqueries, and joins are not universally slow.

walkthrough.title: Filter the timestamp column directly
walkthrough.description: watched_at is the column an index can search. Wrapping it in a function is a different question.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, watched_at FROM watch_events ORDER BY watched_at LIMIT 8;

walkthrough.title: Execute a complete script
walkthrough.description: All setup and the final result run together in one disposable database.

hints: Use >= start and < the next boundary without wrapping watched_at.
Inspect the plan; do not infer speed just from the SQL spelling.

quiz.q: Which filter can search an index on watched_at?
options: A half-open range written on watched_at itself
A function wrapped around watched_at, such as date(watched_at)
A comparison that never mentions watched_at
quiz.why: A range on the bare column can SEARCH an index. Wrapping the column in a function often forces a scan unless you add an expression index.

challenges.prompt: Create idx_watch_time on watched_at; return id and watched_at for Jan 2025 using a half-open timestamp range.

LEFT JOIN ai_requests r ON r.account_id=a.id GROUP BY a.id;

lessons.title: Silver: clean, map & deduplicate
lessons.reason: Builds cleaned latest customer rows, then summarizes mapped countries; second retains its prerequisite TEMP-table contract.
lessons.concept: Silver applies explicit quality rules. Normalize keys and text, keep the latest customer version, map country codes, and exclude missing keys. With equal version timestamps production logic needs an additional reliable tie-breaker; this sample has none.
lessons.example:
CREATE TEMP TABLE silver_customers AS WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY TRIM(raw_id) ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM bronze_customers WHERE raw_id IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(raw_id)<>'') SELECT TRIM(raw_id) AS customer_id,TRIM(name) AS name,CASE UPPER(TRIM(country)) WHEN 'US' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'USA' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'UK' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'GB' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'IND' THEN 'India' WHEN 'CA' THEN 'Canada' ELSE UPPER(TRIM(country)) END AS country FROM ranked WHERE rn=1;
SELECT customer_id,name,country FROM silver_customers;

walkthrough.title: Profile duplicate natural keys
walkthrough.description: Bronze keeps every source version. Silver will trim keys, map countries, and keep the latest updated_at per key.

FROM bronze_customers
WHERE raw_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY TRIM(raw_id)
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

SELECT customer_id,name,country FROM silver_customers;

To drop every row that ever had a duplicate
quiz.why: Silver normalizes and deduplicates source versions. Ordering newest-first and keeping rn = 1 retains one current row per trimmed key. Surrogate keys belong to later Gold modeling.

lessons.title: Gold: dimensions, facts & quality gates
lessons.reason: Accepted fact construction transfers to reconciliation of rejected rows; state validation checks the built table.
lessons.concept: Gold presents business entities and measures. Dimensional surrogate keys come from the existing dimension lookup, not a new ROW_NUMBER on every load. One fact row is one sales line. For this exercise reject unknown keys, invalid dates, and nonpositive/nonnumeric quantities; recompute sales from quantity × catalog price.
lessons.example:
CREATE TEMP TABLE built_fact AS SELECT b.row_id AS sale_key,c.customer_key,p.product_key,CAST(b.quantity AS INTEGER) AS quantity,CAST(b.quantity AS INTEGER)*p.price AS sales,b.order_date FROM bronze_sales b JOIN dim_customer c ON c.customer_id=TRIM(b.customer_id) JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_id=TRIM(b.product_id) WHERE TRIM(b.quantity)<>'' AND TRIM(b.quantity) NOT GLOB '*[^0-9]*' AND CAST(b.quantity AS INTEGER)>0 AND b.order_date GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]' AND date(b.order_date,'+0 days')=b.order_date;

lessons.title: Monthly change & cumulative reports
lessons.reason: Monthly cumulative sales transfer to percentage change; comparison is previous observed month, not necessarily previous calendar month.
lessons.concept: Aggregate to monthly grain before using LAG or a running SUM. A percentage change needs a nonzero prior value. This report uses observed months; a complete calendar would be required if missing months should appear as zero.
lessons.example:
WITH monthly AS(SELECT strftime('%Y-%m',order_date) AS month,
SUM(sales) AS sales FROM fact_sales GROUP BY month)
SELECT month,sales,SUM(sales) OVER(ORDER BY month ROWS
UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_sales FROM monthly;

lessons.title: Validate calendar dates before converting
lessons.reason: Format-plus-calendar validation transfers to rejected-row selection; date-shaped invalid dates are explicitly tested.
lessons.concept: Eight digits do not prove a valid date. Shape YYYYMMDD to YYYY-MM-DD, require exactly eight digits, and compare the candidate to SQLite date(candidate,+0 days) so normalization exposes impossible dates. Invalid or missing values remain NULL; keep the source row. SQL Server uses TRY_CONVERT with an explicit style.
lessons.example: WITH shaped AS(SELECT row_id,raw_date,SUBSTR(raw_date,1,4)||'-'||SUBSTR(raw_date,5,2)||'-'||SUBSTR(raw_date,7,2) AS candidate FROM raw_dates) SELECT row_id,raw_date,CASE WHEN raw_date GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]' AND date(candidate,'+0 days')=candidate THEN candidate ELSE NULL END AS clean_date FROM shaped

lessons.reason: Reasoned quarantine transfers to accepted/rejected reconciliation; each source row must belong to exactly one outcome.
lessons.concept: Filtering invalid rows is not enough: preserve a reject table with source identity, raw value, and reason. Accepted + rejected must equal source count with no overlap. This lab classifies only dates: missing, format, or calendar errors. Nothing edits the raw input.
lessons.example: CREATE TEMP TABLE checked_dates AS WITH shaped AS(SELECT row_id,raw_date,SUBSTR(raw_date,1,4)||'-'||SUBSTR(raw_date,5,2)||'-'||SUBSTR(raw_date,7,2) AS candidate FROM raw_dates) SELECT row_id,raw_date,CASE WHEN raw_date GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]' AND date(candidate,'+0 days')=candidate THEN candidate ELSE NULL END AS clean_date FROM shaped; CREATE TEMP TABLE date_rejects AS SELECT row_id,raw_date,CASE WHEN raw_date IS NULL THEN 'missing' WHEN raw_date NOT GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]' THEN 'format' ELSE 'calendar' END AS reason FROM checked_dates WHERE clean_date IS NULL; SELECT row_id,raw_date,reason FROM date_rejects;

lessons.title: Automated star-schema quality tests
lessons.reason: Four independent quality counts transfer to a publish gate; zero orphans alone is insufficient.
lessons.concept: A quality test has a named expectation and a failure count. Zero means that expectation passed, not that all data is perfect. Check unique line IDs, valid measures, and both dimension relationships. Gate promotion on declared blocking rules; do not silently repair financial data.

lessons.title: Idempotent incremental UPSERT & stale updates

lessons.title: Capstone: integrated customers to trusted sales
lessons.reason: Integrated customer reporting transfers to country totals; shared validated TEMP outputs support deliberate capstone consolidation.
lessons.concept: Build two reusable temporary outputs in one script: integrated CRM/ERP customers and validated sales lines with existing dimension keys. Report at customer grain, preserving customers with no valid sales. The catalog states field authority and exercise sales rules. This is a runnable miniature of the architecture, not a deployed enterprise pipeline.
lessons.example:
CREATE TEMP TABLE integrated_customers AS WITH crm AS(WITH ranked AS (SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY TRIM(customer_id) ORDER BY updated_at DESC,source_row DESC) AS rn FROM crm_people WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(customer_id)<>'') SELECT TRIM(customer_id) AS customer_id,TRIM(name) AS name,CASE UPPER(TRIM(gender)) WHEN 'F' THEN 'Female' WHEN 'M' THEN 'Male' ELSE NULL END AS crm_gender FROM ranked WHERE rn=1),erp AS(SELECT CASE WHEN SUBSTR(TRIM(erp_id),1,3)='NAS' THEN SUBSTR(TRIM(erp_id),4) ELSE TRIM(erp_id) END AS customer_id,CASE UPPER(TRIM(gender)) WHEN 'F' THEN 'Female' WHEN 'FEMALE' THEN 'Female' WHEN 'M' THEN 'Male' WHEN 'MALE' THEN 'Male' ELSE NULL END AS erp_gender,birth_date FROM erp_people),loc AS(SELECT REPLACE(TRIM(erp_id),'-','') AS customer_id,CASE UPPER(TRIM(country_code)) WHEN 'US' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'USA' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'GB' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'UK' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'IND' THEN 'India' ELSE 'Unknown' END AS country FROM erp_locations) SELECT c.customer_id,c.name,COALESCE(c.crm_gender,e.erp_gender,'Unknown') AS gender,COALESCE(l.country,'Unknown') AS country,CASE WHEN e.birth_date GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]' AND date(e.birth_date,'+0 days')=e.birth_date AND e.birth_date<='2025-04-01' THEN e.birth_date ELSE NULL END AS birth_date FROM crm c LEFT JOIN erp e ON e.customer_id=c.customer_id LEFT JOIN loc l ON l.customer_id=c.customer_id; CREATE TEMP TABLE built_sales AS SELECT b.row_id AS sale_key,c.customer_key,p.product_key,CAST(b.quantity AS INTEGER) AS quantity,CAST(b.quantity AS INTEGER)*p.price AS sales,b.order_date FROM bronze_sales b JOIN dim_customer c ON c.customer_id=TRIM(b.customer_id) JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_id=TRIM(b.product_id) WHERE TRIM(b.quantity)<>'' AND TRIM(b.quantity) NOT GLOB '*[^0-9]*' AND CAST(b.quantity AS INTEGER)>0 AND b.order_date GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]' AND date(b.order_date,'+0 days')=b.order_date;
SELECT i.customer_id,i.name,i.gender,i.country,COUNT(s.sale_key) AS sales_lines,COALESCE(SUM(s.sales),0) AS total_sales FROM integrated_customers i JOIN dim_customer c ON c.customer_id=i.customer_id LEFT JOIN built_sales s ON s.customer_key=c.customer_key GROUP BY i.customer_id,i.name,i.gender,i.country;
